fn.478: It must be remembered that, according to Aristotle, the best definition, that is to say, that which reveals the essence of a thing, is one which at the same time reveals its cause ([[t:0]]Posterior Analytics[[t:1]], Book II, chap. 10). It follows thence that whatsoever is primitive and simple cannot be defined, for definition does presuppose somewhat general encompassing the particular object to be defined, whereas the primitive being has naught general preceding it or constituting its cause. Vide [[t:10]]Metaph.[[t:11]], Book VIII, chap. 6: [[t:12]]Ὅσα δὲ μὴ ἔχει ὕλην, μήτε νοητὴν μήτε αἰσθητήν, εὐθὺς ὅπερ ἕν τι εἶναί ἐστιν ἕϰαστον, ὥςπερ ϰαὶ ὅπερ ὄν τι, τὸ τόδε, τὸ ποιόν, τὸ ποσόν. διὸ ϰαὶ οὐϰ ἔνεστιν ἐν τοῖς ὁρισμοῖς οὔτε τὸ ὂν οὔτε τὸ ἕν · ϰαὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι εὐθὺς ἕν τί ἐστιν ὥςπερ ϰαὶ ὄν τι. διὸ ϰαὶ οὐϰ ἔστιν ἕτερόν τι αἴτιον τοῦ ἓν εἶναι οὐθενὶ τούτων, οὐδὲ τοῦ ὄν τι εἶναι[[t:13]]. Time is therefore the [[t:16]]number[[t:17]] of motion, according to the [[t:18]]before[[t:19]] and the [[t:20]]after[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]ἀ ρ ι θ μ ὸ ς ϰινήσεως ϰατὰ τὸ πρότερον ϰαὶ ὕστερον. fn.538: It is well to recall here what the author states elsewhere concerning the rational part of the soul, in accordance with Peripatetic theories. In the first of the [[t:0]]Eight Chapters[[t:1]] serving as an introduction to the treatise [[t:2]]Abôth[[t:3]], after having discoursed upon nutrition, sensibility, imagination, and appetition, one finds him expressing himself thus concerning the fifth part of the soul, or the rational faculty (Vide Pococke’s [[t:4]]Porta Mosis[[t:5]], pp. 188 and 189): “The [[t:6]]rational part[[t:7]] is that faculty existing in man by which he is [[t:8]]intelligent[[t:9]], by which reflection is performed, by which he acquires science, and by which he distinguishes between that which is foul and that which is fair, in respect of actions. The actions (of the rational faculty) are some practical, others speculative. The practical pertains to the domain of art or of reflection; the speculative is that by which man knows invariable beings as they are, and this is what is termed [[t:10]]science[[t:11]] in an absolute sense. The artistic faculty is that by which man acquires the arts, as, for example, carpentry, agriculture, medicine, and navigation. Reflection is that by which one examines, in a thing one desires to do, and at the moment one desires to do it, whether it be possible or not to perform it, and, supposing it to be possible, how it ought to be performed.” One perceives that what the author designates as the [[t:12]]rational[[t:13]] or [[t:14]]reasonable[[t:15]] part of the soul is the totality of all those faculties of the soul which belong solely to man; all other faculties, forming the irrational part of the soul, appertain equally to animals. This division of the soul’s faculties into two parts, one reasonable ([[t:16]]τὸ λογιστιϰὸν[[t:17]] or [[t:18]]τὸ λόγον ἔχον[[t:19]]), the other unreasonable ([[t:20]]τὸ ἄλογον[[t:21]]), belongs rather to Plato than to Aristotle; the latter, indeed, seems openly to disapprove of it, in criticising those who affirm that the soul possesses parts (Vide [[t:22]]Treatise on the Soul[[t:23]], Bk. III, chap. 9, and Trendelenburg’s Commentary, on the same chapter, §§ 2 and 3, p. 528). Nevertheless, Aristotle himself makes use of this division in his classification of virtues. See [[t:24]]Eth. Nicom.[[t:25]], Bk. I, chap. 13; Bk. VI, chap. 2: [[t:26]]Πρότερον μέν οὖν ἐλέχθη δύ’ εἶναι μέρη τῆς ψυχῆς, τό τε λόγον ἔχον ϰαὶ τὸ ἄλογον · νῦν δὲ περὶ τοῦ λόγον ἔχοντος τὸν αὐτόν τρόπον διαιρετέον. ϰαὶ ὑποχείσθω δύο τὰ λόγον ἔχοντα, ἕν μὲν ᾧ θεωροῦμεν τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ὄντων ὅσων αἱ ἀρχαὶ μὴ ἐνδέχονται ἄλλως ἔχειν, ἕν δὲ ᾧ τὰ ἐνδεχόμενα · ϰ. τ. λ[[t:27]]. It is this classification which has served as the basis for what Maimonides states concerning the [[t:28]]rational part[[t:29]] of the soul in the passage just cited.

fn.597.sub_0: As the commentator Shem-Tov observes, what the author states here is found nowhere in the [[t:0]]Metaphysics[[t:1]] of Aristotle, but rather the contrary. Indeed, the [[t:2]]one[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]τὸ ὄν[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]in itself[[t:7]], to which Aristotle assigns four principal meanings, namely: the [[t:8]]continuous[[t:9]], the [[t:10]]whole[[t:11]], the [[t:12]]individual[[t:13]], and the [[t:14]]universal[[t:15]] (according as one considers therein the indivisibility of movement or that of the idea), is inseparable from the very nature and quiddity of the thing which is [[t:16]]one[[t:17]], and cannot be regarded as an [[t:18]]accident[[t:19]] of quiddity. The [[t:20]]one[[t:21]] is not in itself an essence, and it can only subsist in a subject. Its proper character is to be indivisible and the first measure in each genus, and notably the measure of quantity; but, just as [[t:22]]being[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]τὸ ὄν[[t:25]]), with which it is confounded and identified, it applies to all the [[t:26]]categories[[t:27]], and is not found particularly in a single one. The [[t:28]]multiple[[t:29]] is opposed to the [[t:30]]one[[t:31]], as the divisible to the indivisible, and not as non-being to being; for the [[t:32]]multiple[[t:33]] is in [[t:34]]being[[t:35]], as well as the [[t:36]]one[[t:37]], and is attributed, like the latter, to all categories. The [[t:38]]one[[t:39]] and the [[t:40]]multiple[[t:41]] in number, designating quantity alone, are abstractions and entirely distinct from [[t:42]]being.[[t:43]] See details in Aristotle's [[t:44]]Metaphysics[[t:45]], book V, chap. 6, and book X, chap. 1 et seq. — Maimonides, who perceives in the [[t:46]]one[[t:47]] and the [[t:48]]multiple[[t:49]] naught but [[t:50]]accidents[[t:51]] distinct from [[t:52]]being[[t:53]], has furthermore followed the opinion of Ibn-Sīnā, who, as Ibn-Rushd observes, confounded the [[t:54]]one[[t:55]] of number with the [[t:56]]absolute one[[t:57]]: «A difficulty one may encounter here,» says Ibn-Rushd ([Lat.: l. c.], book III), «is this: how, admitting that the [[t:58]]one[[t:59]] of number pertains to the category of [[t:60]]quantity[[t:61]], can one subsequently admit that it is found in all categories, and moreover that it is in the categories themselves, and not something merely accessory thereto? It is for this reason that Ibn-Sīnā opined that its substratum must be an [[t:62]]accident[[t:63]] found in all categories.
fn.597.sub_1: Yet it is not thus; for the [[t:64]]one[[t:65]] in number is of a different nature from the other units. Indeed, the [[t:66]]numerical one[[t:67]] is individuality, abstracted from that which is quantity and quality—one means, from that by which the individual is individual; for it is individual only in the sense of [[t:68]]indivisible[[t:69]], and the mind abstracts it from material things, limits it, and takes it for something separate. The [[t:70]]one[[t:71]] in number, the numerical unity, is naught but a thing that the [[t:72]]soul[[t:73]] creates in individual beings, and without the soul there would be neither numerical unity nor number in general, contrary to what obtains for the line and the surface, and, in general, for continuous quantity; it is for this reason that number is, more than anything else, pure of matter. Ibn-Sīnā confounded the nature of the [[t:74]]one[[t:75]], principle of number, with the [[t:76]]absolute one[[t:77]], which embraces all categories, and as the [[t:78]]one[[t:79]], principle of number, is an [[t:80]]accident[[t:81]], he admitted that the [[t:82]]absolute one[[t:83]], which is the same as [[t:84]]being[[t:85]], is also an accident.» Cf. R. Levi ben-Gerson, [[t:86]]Mil’hamôth[[t:87]], book V, 3, chap. 12.

Ritter, [[t:60]]Geschichte der Philosophie[[t:61]], vol. IV, page 573 et seq.). St. Thomas, in his turn, by stating that one can express oneself concerning God only by the [[t:62]]negative way[[t:63]], followed the Arabian philosophers, from whom he doubtless borrowed the term [Lat.: via remotionis] [[t:66]](طريق النفي)[[t:67]]. fn.637.sub_0: This somewhat obscure passage has been diversely interpreted, and commentators appear greatly perplexed in indicating its precise meaning, as one may discern from the varied explanations afforded by Schem-Tob and by Profiat Duran or Ephodi. The simplest meaning, it appears unto me, is this: One could not attribute unto God that which, from our point of view, would be a perfection; for perfections, being ever any [[t:0]]capacities[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ἕξεις[[t:3]]) whatsoever, belong to one of the genera of the category of [[t:4]]quality[[t:5]], and consequently could not be attributed unto God, as results from that which the author has stated in Chapter LII (p. 195), concerning [[t:6]]qualities.[[t:7]] For further explanation, the author adds: [[t:8]]and every capacity exists not in every[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]being[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]endowed with capacity;[[t:13]] that is to say, that in created beings, capacities are somewhat [[t:14]]accidental[[t:15]], not being found equally in all, and not being always [[t:16]]in act[[t:17]] where they are found. [[t:18]]Capacities[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]ἕξεις[[t:21]]), though more durable and more solid than [[t:22]]dispositions[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]διαθέσεις[[t:25]]), are nevertheless naught else but consolidated [[t:26]]dispositions[[t:27]], and designate somewhat which has been [[t:28]]acquired[[t:29]] and which has not always existed in the being endowed therewith (cf. p. 195, note 2). As Aristotle himself affirms, capacities are likewise dispositions; for those who are endowed with capacities are in a manner but [[t:30]]disposed[[t:31]] for these same capacities ([[t:32]]οί μὲν γὰρ ἕξεις ἔχοντες ϰαί διάϰεινταί γέ πως ϰατ’ αὐτἀς. Catég[[t:33]]., chap. 8). Let one add unto this that capacities are oftentimes [[t:34]]opposed[[t:35]] one to another, and cannot coexist in the same subject. It results from all this that, were one to attribute unto God all that which, in respect of us, is a perfection, one would attribute unto Him [[t:36]]acquired[[t:37]] capacities and even [[t:38]]opposed[[t:39]] capacities, one to another, two things equally inadmissible. — Moses of Narbonne, the most profound commentator upon Maimonides, confessing the perplexity which he had long experienced in explaining the author's words, supposs that this entire passage, from these words: [[t:40]]Thus it is clear unto thee, etc.[[t:41]], relats to a passage in the [[t:42]]Metaphysics[[t:43]] (Book.
fn.637.sub_1: XII, chap. 9), where Aristotle states that the intellect perceives nothing other than itself, being incapable of being affected by aught external to it. Maimonides, when speaking here of all that one must [[t:44]]deny[[t:45]] concerning the supreme intellect, or God, would, one presumes, allude to this absolute negation, in God, of any perception which should not have for its object the divine intellect itself. This intellect possesses its perfection within itself, and cannot be affected by aught. By denying that it perceives anything other than itself, one does not attribute imperfection to it; for all perfections are capacities, yet these capacities do not constitute perfection for every being endowed with them. There are many [[t:46]]privations[[t:47]] which are preferable to [[t:48]]capacities;[[t:49]] for, as Aristotle states in the cited passage, [[t:50]]not to see certain things is better than to see them[[t:51]] ([[t:52]]ϰαί γὰρ μὴ ὁρᾶν ἔνιϰ ϰρεῖττον ἢ ὁρᾶν[[t:53]]). Such, in substance, is the interpretation given to our passage by Moses of Narbonne; but one doubts greatly whether it be the true one, and whether there exist a real connection between the words of Maimonides and the aforementioned passage of Aristotle.

fn.785: In other words: He is the [[t:0]]thought[[t:1]], the subject [[t:2]]which thinks[[t:3]] and the object [[t:4]]which is thought[[t:5]], that is to say, He is absolute thought having Himself as its object. The celebrated proposition of which the author speaks, and which has been extensively developed by the Arabian philosophers, harks back to Aristotle, who, in his Metaphysics (Book XII, chaps. 7 and 9), sets forth that in every intelligence in [[t:6]]act[[t:7]], and consequently in the first mover, which is absolute [[t:8]]energy[[t:9]], there is always perfect identity between that which thinks and that which is thought. The first mover, or God, is the supreme thought thinking itself; in Him, thought is itself its object, and divine thought, says Aristotle, is [[t:10]]the thought of thought[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]αὑτòν ἄρϰ νοει̃, εἴπερ ὲστὶ τὸ ϰράτιστον, ϰαὶ ἔστιν ἡ νόησις νοήσεως νόνσις[[t:13]], chap. 9).— The author, after having dwelt at length, in the preceding chapters, upon the necessity of removing from God every species of attribute and all that might impair His absolute unity and simplicity, demonstrates in this chapter that the proposition in question implies no multiplicity in the divine idea, and that, in it, the [[t:14]]intellect[[t:15]], the [[t:16]]intelligent[[t:17]] and the [[t:18]]intelligible[[t:19]] are one and the same thing. Here, as elsewhere, the author follows in the footsteps of the Arabian Peripatetics, and notably of Ibn-Sînâ, his accustomed guide. Cf. the analysis of Ibn-Sînâ’s philosophy provided by Schahrestâni, in his History of Religious and Philosophical Sects, p. 376 et seq. of the Arabic text (German trans., vol. II, p. 255 et seq.).

fn.793.sub_0: The author here approaches a subject which, as he himself states at the close of this chapter, can be properly comprehended only by those familiar with Peripatetic philosophy, and especially that portion pertaining to the soul and its faculties. Without entering here into disquisitions which the confines of a footnote would not admit, it shall be necessary, for the better apprehension of the author's reasoning, to briefly recall the Aristotelian theory of intelligence and the developments this theory has received amongst the Arab philosophers whom our author has taken for his guides. — In considering the diverse faculties of the soul enumerated by Aristotle, one observs therein a successive progression from the less perfect to the more perfect, in such wise that each superior faculty presupposs the inferior faculty, whose action it renders more complete, and that the one is to the other what [[t:0]]energy[[t:1]] or [[t:2]]act[[t:3]] is to [[t:4]]potency[[t:5]], or what form is to matter. One may distinguish three principal faculties of the soul: [[t:6]]nutrition[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]τὸ θρεπτιϰόν[[t:9]] sc. [[t:10]]μόριον[[t:11]]), to which the life of plants is confined; [[t:12]]sensibility[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]τὸ αἰσθητιϰόν[[t:15]]), which pertains to all animals; and [[t:16]]reason[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]τὸ διανοητιϰόν[[t:19]]), which belongs to man alone (Treatise [[t:20]]on the Soul[[t:21]], Book II, chap. 2); the third faculty could not subsist without the second, nor this latter without the first. [[t:22]]Nutrition[[t:23]] has for its object material things; by this faculty the animal does assimilate external things themselves, whereas by [[t:24]]sensibility[[t:25]] it receivs only the forms of things, even as wax receivs only the form of the seal, and not its matter. [[t:26]]Reason[[t:27]], or [[t:28]]thought[[t:29]], is to intelligible things what sensibility is to sensible things; but through the senses one knows only individuals or individual forms; one knows that things exist, but one knows not why they exist; it is reason which discerns general forms and causes. The soul, says Aristotle, that is to say, the intelligent part of the soul, is [[t:30]]the place of forms[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]τόπος εὶδῶν[[t:33]]).
fn.793.sub_1: As it is to govern all, reason possesses no peculiar bodily organ; it must needs be [[t:34]]impassible[[t:35]], that is to say, it must not be affected by external things, but must be [[t:36]]capable[[t:37]] of receiving the form of objects. These forms it does not possess at the outset [[t:38]]in act[[t:39]], that is to say, in full reality, but only [[t:40]]in potency[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]Ibid.[[t:43]], book 3, chapter 4). Just as in all beings one distinguishes, on the one hand, matter, or that which is in potency, and, on the other hand, form, or the cause which brings that which is [[t:44]]in potency[[t:45]] to pass into [[t:46]]act[[t:47]], so also must these differences necessarily be found within the rational part of the soul, or in the intellect. Aristotle, then, distinguishes two [[t:48]]intellects[[t:49]], the one [[t:50]]passive[[t:51]] ([[t:52]]νοῦς παθητιϰός[[t:53]]), the other [[t:54]]active[[t:55]] ([[t:56]]νοῦς ποιητιϰός[[t:57]]). The passive intellect occupies a middle ground between sensibility and imagination, on the one hand, and the active intellect, on the other; it is this latter, above all, which is separate (from the lower faculties of the soul), impassible, unmixed with aught whatsoever, being [[t:58]]in act[[t:59]] by its very essence ([[t:60]]ϰαὶ οὗτος ὁ νοῦς χωριστὸς ϰαὶ ἀπαθὴς ϰαὶ ἀμιγής, τῇ ονσίᾳ ὢν ἐνεργείᾳ[[t:61]]. [[t:62]]Ibid.[[t:63]], chapter 5). Aristotle does not clearly inform us whence this active intellect proceeds, nor how it is perceived by the passive intellect; yet he seems to discern therein something divine, which comes from without by means of the first mover. Vide the treatise on the [[t:64]]Generation of Animals[[t:65]], book II, chapter 3: [[t:66]]λείπεται δὲ τὸν νοῦν μóνον θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι ϰαὶ θει̃ον εἶναι ϰ. τ. λ.[[t:67]]; cf. Trendelenburg, [Lat.: Arist. de Animá], page 496. It is by the aid of this active intellect that every individual intelligence accomplishes the labour of thought, and, passing from [[t:70]]potency[[t:71]] to [[t:72]]act[[t:73]], it appropriates to itself the forms of things and identifies itself therewith. These intelligible forms, the object of thought, are themselves thought; for the intellect in act cannot be affected by aught external to itself, and it must needs draw from within itself that which it holds as its object. The intellect, therefore, in its [[t:74]]entelechy[[t:75]], or in its complete reality, thinks itself. Vide Aristotle, Metaphysics, book XII, chap.
fn.793.sub_2: 7: [[t:76]]αὑτὺν δἐ νοει̃ ὁ νοῦς ϰατὰ μετάληψιν τοῦ νοητοῦ νοητὸς γὰρ γίγνεται θιγγάνων ϰαὶ νοῶν ὣστε ταὐτὸν νοῦς ϰαἰ νοητὀν[[t:77]]. Cf. Treatise [[t:78]]On the Soul[[t:79]], book III, at the close of chapter 4. Such, in substance, is the theory of Aristotle; the obscurity which reigns within this theory, particularly concerning the nature of the active intellect and its union with the passive intellect, has given rise, among commentators, to protracted discussions and the most diverse opinions; and the Arabic philosophers, confounding herein, as elsewhere, the theories of Aristotle with those of his Neoplatonic commentators, have elaborated, upon the subject which now engages our attention, a new doctrine which subsequently spread amongst the Scholastics. Here follows, in summary, the theory of the Arabic philosophers, who differ amongst themselves on several essential points. The [[t:80]]speculative[[t:81]] faculty, or the [[t:82]]theoretic reason[[t:83]], being the highest among the faculties of the rational soul (vide above, page 210, note 1), receivs the impression of forms separated from matter, whether these be general forms which it abstracts from material and individual things, or immaterial and imperishable beings, which are in themselves abstract forms (as, for instance, the [[t:84]]separated intelligences[[t:85]]). This faculty, denominated the [[t:86]]intellect[[t:87]] [[t:88]](عقل)[[t:89]] by pre-eminence, develops gradually, traversing diverse degrees in which the inferior stands to that which is superior to it as matter stands to form, or as potency stands to act. The Arabic philosophers generally distinguish three degrees of development, or three intellects: 1st, The [[t:90]]hylic intellect[[t:91]] or [[t:92]]material intellect[[t:93]] [[t:94]](العقل الهيولانى)[[t:95]], which is the simple [[t:96]]disposition[[t:97]] possessed by the intellect for abstracting forms; it is a mere [[t:98]]potency[[t:99]] which has not yet begun to pass into [[t:100]]act[[t:101]], and which is termed [[t:102]]hylic[[t:103]] because it may be compared to [[t:104]]matter[[t:105]] ([[t:106]]ὕλη[[t:107]]) disposed to receive form. This [[t:108]]hylic intellect[[t:109]] is the [[t:110]]νοῦς παθητιϰός[[t:111]] of Aristotle [[t:112]](العقل المنفعل)[[t:113]] in its entire abstraction.
fn.793.sub_3: The opinions of the Arabian philosophers are divided concerning the nature of the [[t:114]]hyliac intellect:[[t:115]] some, invoking the authority of Alexander of Aphrodisias, perceive therein naught but a pure [[t:116]]disposition[[t:117]] [[t:118]](استعداد)[[t:119]] attaching to the other faculties of the soul, and which is perishable even as they; and this opinion is adopted by Maimonides (vide infra, chap. LXX); others, taking Themistius as their guide, maintain that, since the [[t:120]]passive[[t:121]] or [[t:122]]hyliac intellect[[t:123]] must, according to Aristotle, be [[t:124]]unmixed[[t:125]] ([[t:126]]ἀμιγής[[t:127]]) with the other faculties of the soul, it must needs be a disposition having for its [[t:128]]substratum[[t:129]] a substance separate from the other faculties; for, they contend, were the [[t:130]]intellect in potency[[t:131]] naught but a simple disposition attaching to the other faculties of the soul, its substratum would be somewhat appertaining to a [[t:132]]genus[[t:133]] other than itself; yet that which is disposed to perceive intelligible things can be naught but an [[t:134]]intellect.[[t:135]] Ibn-Roschd, acknowledging on the one hand the inadmissibility of Alexander’s opinion, likewise discerns difficulties in admitting the other opinion, according to which there would exist a separate and eternal substance whose being would consist solely in a [[t:136]]disposition[[t:137]] and in a simple [[t:138]]potency[[t:139]] ([[t:140]]δύναμ·ς[[t:141]]); he therefore chooses a middle course, by uniting the two opinions, as one has set forth elsewhere (vide the article [[t:142]]Ibn-Roschd[[t:143]], in the [[t:144]]Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques[[t:145]], t. III, pp. 166 et 167). 2° The [[t:146]]intellect in act[[t:147]] [[t:148]](العقل بالفعل)[[t:149]] ; this is the intellect which has succeeded in abstracting form from matter, that is to say, which has succeeded in distinguishing, in individual things, that which constitutes their general form, or that by which a thing is what it is. 3° The [[t:150]]acquired intellect[[t:151]] [[t:152]](العقل المستفاد)[[t:153]] ; this is none other than the intellect in act having become, as it were, the property of man, when the [[t:154]]intelligible forms[[t:155]] are ever present in his intelligence, and when he is able to identify himself with them at any moment without fresh effort.
fn.793.sub_4: Having attained unto this degree, human intelligence has ever for its object the pure intelligible forms; it has for its object the knowledge of its own being and that of immaterial beings external to itself, and it does ascend to the knowledge of the [[t:156]]separate intelligences[[t:157]] and of God. In this state, it becoms, as it were, a substance entirely separated from the body (vide infra, at the close of chap. LXXII). Between the [[t:158]]intellect in act[[t:159]] and the [[t:160]]acquired intellect[[t:161]] some Arabian philosophers do furthermore place the [[t:162]]intellect in capacity[[t:163]] [[t:164]](العقل بالملكة)[[t:165]] ; by this they appear to understand the intellect in act having become a [[t:166]]capacity[[t:167]] ([[t:168]]ἓξις[[t:169]], cf. supra, p. 195, notes 1 and 2), and ere it has in reality attained unto the degree of the [[t:170]]acquired intellect[[t:171]] (cf. the work [[t:172]]Ta’rifât[[t:173]] cited in Freytag’s Dictionary, sub voce [Lat.: under the word] [[t:174]]عقل[[t:175]] , and the Analysis of the philosophy of Ibn-Sinâ, in Schahrestâni, p. 418 of the Arabic text, and t. II, p. 317, of the German translation). This is a subtle distinction, the import of which one does not fully comprehend, and which, it would appear, has not been generally admitted; Ibn-Falaquéra, in enumerating the various [[t:176]]intellects[[t:177]] (vide the Appendix to the [[t:178]]Moré-ha-Moré[[t:179]], at the commencement of chap. fn.793.sub_5: It is by the influence of this active intellect that the [[t:204]]acquired intellect[[t:205]] is formed, considered as its [[t:206]]emanation[[t:207]] (whence, in the Hebrew versions, [[t:208]]השכל הנאצל[[t:209]], the emanated intellect), and which in certain elect men attains to a complete identification with the universal active intellect (cf. above, page 277, note 3, and one's article [[t:210]]Ibn-Roschd[[t:211]], [Lat.: loco citato], pages 167 and 169). — One shall, in other places, discourse upon divers details of this theory, the whole of which one has deemed it necessary to present here. It is understood that its obscurity has given rise to numerous divergences of opinion; the hypotheses, which one had sought even in regions inaccessible to the human mind, left a free career to the imagination, and the most enlightened Arab philosophers could not but abandon here the true ground of philosophical speculation, to lose themselves in reveries. "Not a single one," says Ibn-Falaquéra, "has a well-settled opinion upon this subject, and one often observs the same author to change his opinion and to state in one work something altogether different from that which he has stated in another." See [[t:212]]Moré-ha-Moré[[t:213]], book II, chapter 25 (page 111).

This first cause is, according to Aristotle, a necessary condition of science, which would be impossible if causes extended to infinity; for the illimitable escapes science. Cf. fn.827: Aristotle demonstrates, in sundry passages of his [[t:0]]Metaphysics[[t:1]], that primary matter and primary form neither come into being nor perish. Throughout all being, [[t:2]]generation[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]γένεσις[[t:5]]) and [[t:6]]destruction[[t:7]] or [[t:8]]corruption[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]φθορά[[t:11]]) are naught else but [[t:12]]change;[[t:13]] that which comes into being, comes into being from somewhat (which is the matter), by receiving the form (through which alone it is what it is), and it perishes by losing its form. It is manifest, therefore, that the idea of [[t:14]]matter[[t:15]], like that of [[t:16]]form[[t:17]], excluds generation and destruction; for, were matter or form capable of coming into being or perishing, it would be requisite that each of the twain should in turn be compounded of matter and form, a process extending to infinity, did one not halt at a primary matter and a primary form, which, consequently, can neither come into being nor perish. — Maimonides appears here to have especially in view a passage in the VII[[t:18]]th[[t:19]] book of the [[t:20]]Metaphysics[[t:21]] (chap. 8), in which Aristotle does summarily state thus: Since that which comes into being does so [[t:22]]by[[t:23]] somewhat (the efficient cause) and [[t:24]]from[[t:25]] somewhat (the matter), and becoms somewhat (by the [[t:26]]form[[t:27]]), the efficient cause produces neither matter alone nor form alone. He, for instance, who fashions a sphere of bronze, makes neither the bronze nor the spherical form in itself, but does impart this form unto the bronze, which is its [[t:28]]substratum[[t:29]]. Were the efficient cause truly to produce this form in itself, the latter would in turn come into being [[t:30]]from[[t:31]] somewhat, and would likewise be compounded of matter and form, and [[t:32]]generations[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]γενέσεις[[t:35]]) would continue ad infinitum. It is manifest, therefore, that [[t:36]]form[[t:37]], or that which in sensible things one may denominate [[t:38]]figure[[t:39]], does not [[t:40]]come into being;[[t:41]] there is, consequently, no [[t:42]]generation[[t:43]] for it, nor for the [[t:44]]what[[t:45]] in itself ([[t:46]]τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι[[t:47]]), which always comes into being in something else, be it by art, or by nature, or by a faculty. Here are Aristotle's own words: [[t:48]]εἰ οὖν ϰαὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖ αὺτό[[t:49]] (sc., [[t:50]]τὸ εἶδος[[t:51]]), [[t:52]]δῆλον ὃτι ὡσαύτως ποιήσει ϰαί βαδιοῦνται αἱ γενέσεις εἰς ἄπειρον. φανεὸν ἄρα ὃτι οὐδέ τὸ εἶδος, ἢ ὁτιδήποτε χρὴ ϰαλεῖν τὴν ἐν τῷ αἰσθητῷ μορφήν, γίγνεται, οὐδ’ ἒστιν αὐτοῦ γένεσις, οὐδὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι. τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ὃ ἐν ἄλλῳ γίγνεται ἢ ὑπὸ τέχνης ἢ ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ δυνάμεως[[t:53]]. Vide also [[t:54]]Metaph[[t:55]]., VII, 15; VIII, 3, 5; XII, 3. It is perceived that the matter at hand is indeed, as Maimonides does state, all form in general, or the [[t:56]]physical[[t:57]] form, inseparable from matter, and not merely the absolute [[t:58]]primary form,[[t:59]] or the prime mover.

The import is this: that the doctors, to prove that the other things they have enumerated likewise exist in [[t:38]]’Arabôth[[t:39]], restrict themselves to citing Scriptural passages where these things are directly attributed to God; for naught emanates from God save through the intermediation of [[t:40]]’Arabôth[[t:41]], which, as has been observed, is the instrument by which God governs the universe. Thus, for example, to demonstrate that [[t:42]]’Arabôth[[t:43]] contains [[t:44]]treasures of life[[t:45]], one cits these words of the Psalmist: [[t:46]]For with Thee is the fountain of life[[t:47]] (Ps. 36, 10); for [[t:48]]the treasures of peace[[t:49]], one cits this passage: [[t:50]]And he called it[[t:51]] (the altar) [[t:52]]the Eternal God of peace[[t:53]] (Judges, 6, 24); for [[t:54]]the treasures of blessing: He shall receive the blessing from the Lord[[t:55]] (Ps. 24, 5), and so forth. Vide [[t:56]]’Haghîgâ[[t:57]], [Lat.: loc. cit.]. — In the editions of Ibn-Tibbon’s version (with the exception of the [Lat.: editio princeps] [[t:59]]), our passage is found translated twice, firstly literally, then in a manner that more clearly conveys its sense; the second translation is expressed in these terms: [[t:60]]ובן הביאו ראיה על השאר שהם בערבות מהיותם מיוחסים לשם יתעלה[[t:61]] (the words [[t:62]]שהם אצלו[[t:63]], which the editions add, are repeated from the first translation and ought to be effaced).
fn.864.sub_1: Most manuscripts and the [Lat.: editio princeps] [[t:65]] contain only this second translation, which Ibn-Tibbon had placed in the margin, adding thereto the following note found in some manuscripts: [[t:66]]אמר שמואל בן חבון הלשון המוגה מחוץ אינו יוצא מלשון הערכי אך הוא יוצא מגוף הענין מלשון חגיגה והוא האמת בעצמו והוא שהעיר עליו באמרו והבן זה[[t:67]] «Samuel Ibn-Tibbon says: The rectified reading which is found without does not correspond to the Arabic text, but rather proceeds from the very subject contained within the text of [[t:68]]’Haghîgâ;[[t:69]] this is the veritable sense, and this is what the author has indicated by saying: [[t:70]]One must understand this[[t:71]].»
fn.871: That is to say, the metaphysical subjects which have been discussed in the preceding chapters, and which have been designated by the Rabbins under the denomination of [[t:0]]Ma’asé mercabâ[[t:1]] (consult the preceding chapter, and supra, p. 9). — Before exposing, in the II[[t:2]]nd[[t:3]] part of this work, the doctrines of the philosophers concerning the existence of God, His unity, and His incorporeality, the author will, in the final chapters of this I[[t:4]]st[[t:5]] part, present an exposition of the system of the [[t:6]]Motécallemîn[[t:7]]. The present chapter, serving as an introduction to this exposition, does contain sundry historical indications regarding the origin of the said system, the influence of which is perceptible amongst certain Jewish theologians of the Orient. The author does intimate, at the commencement of this chapter, that philosophical sciences had been cultivated by the ancient Jews, and that the metaphysical subjects in question were not familiar to them solely through religious tradition. Whatever may be the value of this assertion, it is in conformity with the opinion of sundry ancient authors, and one has elsewhere demonstrated that this opinion has been upheld by pagan, Christian, and Muslim writers. Consult one's article [[t:8]]Juifs[[t:9]], in the [[t:10]]Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques[[t:11]], t. III, p. 352, and the notes appended thereto in the [[t:12]]Archives israélites[[t:13]], number for March 1848 (the whole published separately in German, with additions, by Dr. B. Beer, under the title of: [[t:16]]Philosophie und philosophische Schriftsteller der Juden[[t:17]], Leipzig, 1852, octavo, pp. 7 and 96). In Maimonides' time, the said opinion was generally accredited, as may be seen in the following passage from Ibn-Roschd, towards the end of his [[t:18]]Destruction de la Destruction[[t:19]] (Hebr. version): [[t:20]]ולא יםפק אחד שהנה היו בבני ישראל חכמים רבים וזה גלוי מהםפרים אשר ימצאו אצל בני ישראל המיוחםים אל שלמה ולא םרה החכמה ענין נמצא באנשי הנבואה והם הנביאים ע״ה[[t:21]] “None does doubt that there were amongst the Israelites many philosophers, and this is evident from the books found amongst the Israelites and attributed unto Solomon. Science has continually existed amongst the inspired men, who are the prophets.”
fn.876: Ibn-Tibbon's version reads [[t:0]]וםפקות נופלות בלשון המחובר בםפר ושגגה תתחבר לו[[t:1]]. It is observed that the translator took [[t:2]]אלמדון[[t:3]] for a passive participle [[t:4]](المدوّن)[[t:5]] signifying [[t:6]]that which has been committed to writing;[[t:7]] it is in the same sense that this word has been rendered by Al-’Harizi. The words [[t:8]]ושגגה תתחבר לן[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]the error which attached itself thereto[[t:11]]) would, according to sundry commentators, signify: the errors of the copyists which were conjoined with the obscurity of the redaction; but the Arabic word [[t:12]]سہوُ[[t:13]] does rather designate an error of [[t:14]]thought[[t:15]] or of [[t:16]]opinion[[t:17]], a [[t:18]]misapprehension[[t:19]]. It appears to one preferable to consider [[t:20]]אלמדון[[t:21]] as an active participle [[t:22]]المدون[[t:23]] , signifying [[t:24]]redactor;[[t:25]] the words [[t:26]]וםהו יצחבה[[t:27]] signify literally [[t:28]]and the misapprehension[[t:29]] or [[t:30]]the error which accompanied it[[t:31]], that is to say, which lay within the mind of the redactor.
fn.880.sub_0: The word [[t:0]]calâm[[t:1]] [[t:2]](كلام)[[t:3]], which signifies [[t:4]]speech[[t:5]] or [[t:6]]discourse[[t:7]], designates also a science which arose among the Muslims from the second century of the Hegira, and which aimed to combat the doctrines of heterodox sects, and later those of the philosophers, by employing against its adversaries the weapons of dialectic and arguments borrowed from the philosophical schools. One may give to this science the name of [[t:10]]dogmatics[[t:11]], or of rational theology, and it bears much analogy to Christian [[t:12]]scholasticism[[t:13]]. The [[t:14]]calâm[[t:15]] developed especially since the introduction, among the Arabs, of Peripatetic philosophy, and one will see further on (chap. LXXIII et seq.) what doctrines were established by this science and how they proceeded to demonstrate the truth of the principal religious dogmas, notably those which establish the unity and immateriality of God and Creation. As for the name [[t:16]]calâm[[t:17]], the Arabs themselves are not agreed upon its origin; according to some, the said science was thus called because in it one had at first discussed principally what was to be understood by [[t:18]]divine speech[[t:19]] or by the [[t:20]]speech[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]calâm[[t:23]]) attributed to God (cf. infra, p. 343, note 3); according to others, the word [[t:24]]calâm[[t:25]] would be but an imitation of the word [[t:26]]mantik[[t:27]] [[t:28]](منطق)[[t:29]], which likewise signifies [[t:30]]speech[[t:31]], or [[t:32]]discourse[[t:33]], and by which the philosophers designated one of the principal branches of their doctrine, namely, [[t:34]]logic[[t:35]]. See Schahrestâni, [[t:36]]History of Religious and Philosophical Sects[[t:37]], Arab. text, p. 18 (Germ. transl., vol. I, p. 26); cf. Pococke, [[t:38]]Specimen hist. ar[[t:39]]., p. 195. From the word [[t:40]]calâm[[t:41]] comes the verb [[t:42]]técallam[[t:43]] [[t:44]](تكلم)[[t:45]], bearing the sense of [[t:46]]to profess the calâm[[t:47]], and of which the participle [[t:48]]motécallem[[t:49]], in the plural [[t:50]]motécallémîn[[t:51]], designates the adherents of [[t:52]]calâm[[t:53]].
fn.880.sub_1: Having regard to the sense of [[t:54]]speech[[t:55]] that the word [[t:56]]calâm[[t:57]] possesses, the Hebrew translators denominated this science [[t:58]]חכמת הדבר[[t:59]] and designated the Motécallémîn by the name of [[t:60]]Medabberim[[t:61]] ([[t:62]]מדברים[[t:63]]), which the Latin translators, in their turn, rendered by [Lat.: loquentes]. One may also see what one has said concerning the [[t:66]]calâm[[t:67]] in the [[t:68]]Dictionary of Philosophical Sciences[[t:69]], vol. I, art. [[t:70]]Arabs[[t:71]] (pp. 169 and 174), and in one’s [[t:72]]Notice sur R. Saadia Gaôn[[t:73]], p. 16 et seq. (M. Cahen’s Bible, vol. IX, pp. 88 et seq.). — The two Hebrew translators have not well apprehended the sense that the word [[t:74]]אלכלאם[[t:75]] bears in our passage, and they have taken it in its primitive sense of [[t:76]]speech[[t:77]] or [[t:78]]discourse;[[t:79]] Ibn-Tibbon translates: [[t:80]]מדברי ענין היחוד[[t:81]], and Al-’Harizi: [[t:82]]מדבריהם בענין היחוד[[t:83]]. Following the words which one has just cited, one must read, in Ibn-Tibbon’s version: [[t:84]]ומה שנתלה בזה הענין[[t:85]], as the manuscripts and the [Lat.: editio princeps] have it; in the other editions, there has been erroneously inserted: [[t:88]]ומה שנתגלה מזה הענין[[t:89]].
fn.881: It is known that the title of [[t:0]]Gaôn[[t:1]] [[t:2]]גאון[[t:3]] (in the plural [[t:4]]Geonim[[t:5]]) was borne by the heads of the Jewish academies of Babylonia, under Arab dominion, from the close of the seventh [[t:6]]century[[t:7]] until approximately the middle of the eleventh [[t:8]]century[[t:9]]. The period of the [[t:10]]Geonim[[t:11]] coincides with that of the development of the [[t:12]]Kalām[[t:13]] amongst the Arabs; the example afforded by the Muslim theologians was followed by certain Jewish doctors of the East, who, like the [[t:14]]Mutakallimūn[[t:15]], endeavoured to uphold religious dogmas through philosophical speculation, and laid the foundations of a systematic and rational theology. It was the doctors of the Karaite sect who first embarked upon this path and themselves adopted the appellation of [[t:16]]Mutakallimūn[[t:17]] ([Lat.: vide] the [[t:18]]Khozari[[t:19]], book V, § 15), without, however, assenting to all the hypotheses of Muslim [[t:20]]Kalām[[t:21]], which shall be expounded further on (chap. LXXIII). Some Rabbanite doctors amongst the [[t:22]]Geonim[[t:23]] imitated the example of the Karaites (cf. above, p. 286, note 3, and p. 290, note 2). There remains to us, in the [[t:24]]Book of Beliefs and Opinions[[t:25]] by Rabbi Saadia Gaon, a significant monument of what one may term Jewish [[t:26]]Kalām[[t:27]], and it is to this celebrated doctor that Maimonides appears here to allude, as Moïse de Narbonne observes in his commentary upon our passage. In vol. III of the [[t:28]]Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques[[t:29]], under the article [[t:30]]Juifs[[t:31]] (p. 355-357), one has provided further details on this subject. One would add, moreover, that Arab authors of the tenth [[t:32]]century[[t:33]] expressly speak of Jewish [[t:34]]Mutakallimūn[[t:35]]. Al-Masʿūdī cites several whom he had personally known ([Lat.: vide] Silv. de Sacy, [[t:36]]Notices et Extraits des manuscrits[[t:37]], vol. VIII, p. 167). Isa ibn-Zara’a, a Christian Arab author from Baghdad, speaking, in his theological opuscules, of a certain Abu’l-Khayr Daud ibn-Mushajj, states that he was one of the foremost Jewish [[t:38]]Mutakallimūn[[t:39]] and a profound thinker [[t:40]](...من متكلّمي اليهود وكان متقدّما فيهم نظّارا)[[t:41]] . [Lat.: Vide] ms. ar. of the Imperial Library, old collection, no. 98, fol. 40 [[t:42]]b[[t:43]] and 42 [[t:44]]a[[t:45]].
fn.882: The sect of the [[t:0]]Muʿtazilites[[t:1]] [[t:2]](المعتزلة)[[t:3]], whose name signifies [[t:4]]separatists[[t:5]] or [[t:6]]dissidents[[t:7]], had as its founder Wāṣil ibn-ʿAṭā (born in the year 80 A.H., or 699-700 C.E., and deceased in the year 131 A.H., or 748-749 C.E.). Wāṣil, a disciple of Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (from Basra), having [[t:8]]separated[[t:9]] [[t:10]](اعتزل)[[t:11]] from the school concerning some religious dogma, constituted himself the head of a new school, and established a doctrine whose elements were borrowed from various preceding sects (cf. Shahristānī, p. 18 et seq.; Ger. trans., vol. I, p. 25 et seq.; Pococke, [[t:12]]Specimen hist. ar[[t:13]]., p. 211 et seq.). The Muʿtazilites, subdivided into several branches, are all in agreement upon the two following points: 1° Man possesses perfect liberty in his actions; he performs good and evil by his own volition, and thereby accrues merits or demerits. 2° God, absolutely [[t:14]]one[[t:15]], possesses no attributes distinct from His essence (cf. above, p. 209, note 1). It is on account of these two principal tenets of their doctrine, aiming to establish the absolute justice and unity of God, that the Muʿtazilites designate themselves by the appellation of [[t:16]]أصحاب العدل والتوحيد[[t:17]] (partisans of [[t:18]]justice[[t:19]] and [[t:20]]unity[[t:21]] ). These are precisely the same expressions which the Arab historian Al-Masʿūdī employs to designate the doctrine of the disciples of ʿAnān ([Lat.: vide] de Sacy, [[t:22]]Notices et Extraits[[t:23]], [Lat.: loc. cit.]; [[t:24]]Chrest. ar[[t:25]]., vol. I, p. 349-351), a circumstance which proves that the Karaite theologians principally took as their model the Muslim doctors of the sect of the [[t:26]]Muʿtazilites[[t:27]]. In accord with Maimonides, the Karaite author Ahron ben-Eliya expressly states that the Karaite scholars and a portion of the Rabbanites adhered to the doctrines of the [[t:28]]Muʿtazilites[[t:29]] ([Lat.: vide] [[t:30]]עץ חיים[[t:31]] or [[t:32]]Tree of Life[[t:33]], Leipzig edition, p. 4).
fn.883: The [[t:0]]Ash'ariyyah[[t:1]] or Ash'arites are the disciples of Abu'l-Hasan 'Ali ibn-Isma'il al-[[t:2]]Ash'ari[[t:3]] of Basra (born around the year 880 of the Christian era, and deceased in 940). This individual, brought up in the principles of the Mu'tazilah, and already one of their principal doctors, publicly declared, upon a Friday, in the great mosque of Basra, that he repented having professed heretical doctrines, and that he acknowledged the pre-existence of the Qur'an, the attributes of God, and the predestination of human actions. The Ash'arites, therefore, unreservedly admitted attributes of God distinct from His essence and denied the free will of man. It is evident that their doctrine was diametrically opposed to that of the Mu'tazilah; they nevertheless made certain reservations to avoid falling into anthropomorphism and not to deny all species of merit and demerit in human actions (vide the article [[t:4]]Arabes[[t:5]] in the [[t:6]]Dictionnaire des sc. philos[[t:7]]., vol. I, page 176, and cf. above, page 186, note 1). Several details of the Ash'arite doctrine shall be expounded further on, chap. LXXIII (Prop. 6, 7 etc.); concerning the absolute fatalism professed by this sect, vide the III[[t:8]]rd[[t:9]] part of this work, chap. XVII (3[[t:10]]rd[[t:11]] opinion).
fn.885: It would appear to result from Maimonides' statement here that, prior to his era, a certain number of Jewish theologians or philosophers had existed in Andalusia or Muslim Spain (cf. above, chap. XLII, page 149, and [[t:0]]ibid.[[t:1]], note 1), but that already in his time, only a small number of works, emanating from a few recent writers, of the philosophical literature of the Jews of Spain were still extant. Those which remain to us even at present generally justify the judgement rendered by our author, with the exception of two who have drawn various borrowings from the Mutakallimun. Solomon ibn-Gabirol of Malaga has bequeathed unto us, in his [[t:2]]Source of Life[[t:3]], an important document which proves that from the XI[[t:4]]th[[t:5]] century, and before Peripatetic philosophy had found a worthy representative amongst the Muslims of Spain, the Jews of that country had successfully devoted themselves to philosophical studies and had approached the highest metaphysical questions; and from that same epoch there were also in Spain writers who deemed it their duty to defend religion against the encroachments of philosophy. Cf. my [[t:6]]Notice sur Abou’l-Walîd Merwân ibn-Djanâ’h[[t:7]], page 81 et seq. ([[t:8]]Journal asiatique[[t:9]], July 1850, page 45 et seq.). Around 1160, Abraham ben-David of Toledo, an adversary of Ibn-Gabirol, undertook, in his work entitled [[t:10]]The Sublime Faith[[t:11]], to reconcile religion and philosophy; and one discerns in him a great admirer of Aristotle's philosophy, which he introducs into religious questions in almost the same measure as Maimonides. Around the same period, Judah ha-Levi of Castile had, in his celebrated [[t:12]]Kuzari[[t:13]], declared war upon philosophy, in which he was profoundly versed; yet at the same time, he had rejected the reasonings of the [[t:14]]Kalam[[t:15]], which he regarded as useless subtleties (vide his aforesaid work, book V, § 16). Amongst his contemporaries, Moses ben-Jacob ibn-Ezra appears to belong to the philosophical school, whereas Joseph ibn-Saddiq was in diverse respects under the influence of the [[t:16]]Kalam[[t:17]] (cf. above, page 209, note 1). This same influence is discernible, at the close of the XI[[t:18]]th[[t:19]] century, in the celebrated work of Ba'hya ben-Joseph of Saragossa, entitled [[t:20]]Duties of the Hearts;[[t:21]] in the I[[t:22]]st[[t:23]] book, which treats of the [[t:24]]Unity of God[[t:25]], one discovers several arguments borrowed from the [[t:26]]Mutakallimun[[t:27]] (see notably chapter V), although, in respect of divine attributes, Ba'hya does show himself entirely in accord with the philosophers (cf. above, page 238, note 1).
fn.886: The author makes allusion to the ecclesiastical writers, Greek and Syriac, who, from the VI[[t:0]]th[[t:1]] century onwards, were constrained to defend Christian dogmas against the increasingly dominant Peripatetic philosophy and against the numerous heresies issuing from that same philosophy. The defenders of religion availed themselves of the weapons of dialectic which the study of Aristotle's philosophy had placed in their hands. Cf. Brucker, [[t:2]]Hist. crit. philos[[t:3]]., vol. III, page 534; Ritter, [[t:4]]Geschichte der Philosophie[[t:5]], vol. VI, page 458 et seq. ([[t:6]]Philos. chrét[[t:7]]., book VII, chap. 1). The same method, as the author is about to explain, was pursued by the Muslim [[t:8]]Mutakallimun[[t:9]], who were acquainted with the writings of several authors of the Greek Church, such as John Philoponus, John Damascene, and others, and who were even more capable of drawing from the writings of Christian theologians of Syria and Mesopotamia. Learned Christians, both Nestorians and Jacobites, lived in great numbers amongst the Muslims, who owed to them their knowledge of the philosophy and sciences of the Greeks. Cf. Wenrich, [Lat.: De auctorum Grœcorum versionibus et commentariis syriacis arabicis etc.], page 7-22; E. Renan, [Lat.: De Philosophia peripatetica apud Syros], Paris 1852.
fn.887: Literally: [[t:0]]when the Christian nation embraced[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]within its bosom[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]these nations[[t:5]] [[[t:6]]and the assertion of the Christians is that which is known[[t:7]]] [[t:8]]etc.[[t:9]] The word [[t:10]]מלה̈[[t:11]] [[t:12]](ملة)[[t:13]], [[t:14]]nation[[t:15]], denotes chiefly a great religious community. In lieu of [[t:16]]דעוי[[t:17]] (assertion), some manuscripts bear the verb [[t:18]]אדעוא[[t:19]] [[t:20]](ادّعوا)[[t:21]]; likewise Ibn-Tibbon: [[t:22]]וטענו הנוצרים מה שכנר נודע[[t:23]], [[t:24]]and the Christians affirmed[[t:25]] (or [[t:26]]maintained[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]that which is known[[t:29]]. The author intends to speak of the mysteries of the Incarnation and of the Trinity.
fn.888: This author is John Philoponus, surnamed [[t:0]]the grammarian[[t:1]], who flourished in Alexandria in the sixth and seventh centuries; his commentary upon Aristotle's [[t:6]]Physics[[t:7]] bears the date of the year 333 of the era of Diocletian, or of the Martyrs, which corresponds to the year 617 of the Christian era ([Lat.: vide] Fabricius, Bibliotheca Græca, vol. X, p. 640, 4th edition). The discourses of Philoponus, to which Maimonides here alludes, are, doubtless, his [[t:12]]Refutation[[t:13]] of Proclus's treatise on the eternity of the world, and his [[t:14]]Cosmogony of Moses[[t:15]].
fn.889: Abu-Zakariyya Yahya [[t:0]]IBN[[t:1]]-'A[[t:2]]DI[[t:3]], a Jacobite Christian, from Tikrit in Mesopotamia, lived in Baghdad in the tenth century. He was a disciple of Al-Farabi, and rendered himself celebrated by his Arabic translations of several works by Aristotle and his commentators. According to Al-Kifti's [[t:6]]Tarîkh al-’hocamâ[[t:7]], he died on the 13th of August of the year 1285 of the Seleucids (974 of the Christian era), aged 81 years. Ibn-'Adi likewise composed theological writings, in which he sought to reconcile philosophy with Christian dogmas; thus, for instance, he perceived in the [[t:10]]Trinity[[t:11]] the unity of the intellect, the intelligent, and the intelligible ([Lat.: confer] above, chap. It would appear that Maimonides was not well acquainted with the epoch in which Ibn-'Adi had lived, and believed him to be of greater antiquity, inasmuch as he seems to suppose that the first Muslim [[t:14]]Motécallemîn[[t:15]] had drawn from his writings.

fn.912: This is the author's reasoning: If one admits that the world is [[t:0]]created[[t:1]], it doubtless follows that a creator exists; but one thereby succeeds in establishing naught save the mere [[t:2]]existence[[t:3]] of God, whereas by admitting the [[t:4]]eternity[[t:5]] of the world, one shall possess rigorous demonstrations for establishing simultaneously the immateriality, the unity, and the immutability of God, as shall be seen in the first chapters of the II[[t:6]]nd[[t:7]] part of this work. fn.923: Already Plato, in the Timaeus, presents the universe as a single individual, as an animated and organic whole possessing the spherical form, and this is likewise the basis of Aristotle's cosmology, expounded in the treatise [[t:0]]On the Heavens[[t:1]] and in that [[t:2]]On the World[[t:3]]. The comparison which the author is about to establish between the organism of the universe and that of the human individual is but the reproduction of an idea widely diffused amongst Jewish writers of all epochs, and which finds its source rather in the doctrines of Pythagoras and Plato than in those of Aristotle. The idea of the [[t:4]]macrocosm[[t:5]] and [[t:6]]microcosm[[t:7]], which appears here and there in the allegories of the Talmud and the [[t:8]]Midrashim[[t:9]], was especially developed in the book [[t:10]]Avot[[t:11]] of [[t:12]]Rabbi Nathan[[t:13]] (chap. 31) and in the book [[t:14]]Yetsirah[[t:15]], and embraced by several Jewish philosophers of the Middle Ages; see, for example, the Extracts from the [[t:16]]Fountain of Life[[t:17]] by Ibn-Gabirol, Book III, §§ 6 and 44, and the [[t:18]]‘Olam Katan[[t:19]], or [[t:20]]The Microcosm[[t:21]], by R. Joseph Ibn-Tzaddik (recently published by M. Ad. Jellinek, Leipzig, 1854, octavo), Book II, sect. 1[[t:22]]st[[t:23]]. In our author's work, the comparison aims only to establish the individuality of the universe; it confines itself to ingenious rapprochements and possesses nothing of the symbolic and mystic character which the Kabbalists and certain moralists have imparted to the theory of the microcosm. — The author will present in this chapter the principal points of [[t:24]]physics[[t:25]], as it was taught in the Arabic schools; Aristotle's theories therein are supplemented and developed here and there by those of Ptolemy, Galen, and the Neoplatonists. One cannot enter into the details of the diverse theories summarised by the author, and one must needs confine oneself, in these notes, to elucidating certain points whose comprehension is more particularly requisite for the reader of this work. Various details relating to Peripatetic cosmology and to the system of Ptolemy will be more amply expounded by the author himself in the II[[t:26]]nd[[t:27]] part of this work, and it would be superfluous to dwell upon them at this juncture.

The selfsame author insinuates that Maimonides knew the doctrines of the [[t:34]]Motécallemîn[[t:35]] solely through the false reports of their adversaries; yet it results from Maimonides’s own declaration that he was perfectly acquainted with the doctrines in question, and here, as everywhere else, his assertions are based upon a serious and profound study of the most authentic sources; vide the commencement of chapter LXXIV. It suffices, moreover, to peruse Ibn-Roschd’s [[t:36]]Destruction of the Destruction[[t:37]], which contains numerous particulars concerning the [[t:38]]Motécallemîn[[t:39]], and in which one rediscovers all the propositions enumerated by Maimonides. As for this X[[t:40]]th[[t:41]] proposition, which Maimonides denominates [[t:42]]the base of the science of the Calâm[[t:43]], it is so essential in the system of the [[t:44]]Motécallemîn[[t:45]] that it is impossible to separate it therefrom. fn.1269.sub_0: Regarding infinity in general, vide Aristotle, [[t:0]]Physics[[t:1]], Book III, chapters 4-8; [[t:2]]Metaph.[[t:3]]., Book II, chapter 2; Book XI, chapter 10. Aristotle demonstrates in these various passages that, in nature, the infinitely great [[t:4]]in actuality[[t:5]], that is to say, infinite extension, is inadmissible, and he admits no other infinity than the infinitely small or the infinite divisibility of space, which he designates (as well as the infinitude of abstract number) as the [[t:6]]infinite in potentiality[[t:7]]. Consequently, the universe itself, being the most extended body, is limited in space (vide the treatise [[t:8]]On the Heavens[[t:9]], Book I, chapter 7, where Aristotle concludes by saying: Ὅ[[t:10]]τι μὲν τοίνυν οὐϰ ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα τὸ τοῦ παντὸς ἄπειρον ἐϰ τούτων φανερόν[[t:11]]). The most general demonstration of this first proposition is given in the very definition of body. Aristotle observes that from a [[t:12]]logical[[t:13]] point of view ([[t:14]]λογιϰῶς[[t:15]]), the existence of an infinite body is inadmissible: for, if one's conception of body is that of being limited by surfaces, there can be no unlimited body, whether intelligible or sensible ([[t:16]]εἰ γάρ έστι σώματος λόγος τὸ ἐπιπέδῳ ὡρισμένον, οὐϰ ἂν εἴη σῶμα ἄπειρον, οὔτε νοητὸν οὔτε αἰσθητόν[[t:17]]. [[t:18]]Physics[[t:19]], III, 5, [[t:20]]Metaph.[[t:21]]., XI, 10). From a [[t:22]]physical[[t:23]] point of view, Aristotle demonstrates that an infinite body could be neither composite nor simple: 1° Were it composite, the parts of the composition would be either infinite or finite; now it is evident that they could not be infinite, for the infinitude of each necessarily excludes that of the others; but neither could they be finite, for they would be consumed by the infinite, and would entirely disappear before it. 2° Neither could the infinite body be simple; for none of the elements, each of which has its determined region, is infinite, and there exists no sensible body, outside of the elements, which unites them all, as several physicists have believed.— Another physical proof (which in some sort relates to the logical proof) is this: «Every sensible body is in space. The species and differences of space are: up and down, front and back, right and left. These distinctions exist not merely in relation to us and by position, but are founded in the whole itself.
fn.1269.sub_1: Yet they could not exist in the infinite.» (Vide [[t:24]]Physics, l. c.[[t:25]] at the end of chapter 5). Ibn-Sînâ and other authors, both Arabic and Jewish, have multiplied the demonstrations of the propositions enumerated by Maimonides. Abou-becr-Mo’hammed al-Tebrizi, who composed a commentary upon the twenty-five propositions, entered into lengthy details to demonstrate their truth. This 1[[t:26]]st[[t:27]] proposition has been demonstrated by the Arabs in several different ways. One shall here cite a demonstration borrowed from Ibn-Sînâ: Let the magnitude supposed infinite be a line AB [[t:28]]أ ج ب[[t:29]]; one may suppose this line to be prolonged to infinity on both sides or only on one side B. In this latter case, let one imagine that from the finite side a part AC is cut; one shall then have two lines AB and CB, each of which will be infinite on side B and finite on the other side. Now, if one superimposes point C upon point A, one of two things must follow: either the line CB will be prolonged to infinity like the line AB, and then one shall have AB—AC=AB, which is impossible, for the part cannot be equal to the whole; or else the line CB will be prolonged less than the line AB, and then it will be finite on side B, which is contrary to the hypothesis. If the line AB is supposed infinite on both sides, it may be cut at any point whatsoever, so as to form two lines, each of which will be infinite on one side and finite on the other, and the demonstration will be the same as that just given. Cf. Schahrestâni, p. 403 (German transl., vol. [[t:30]]II[[t:31]], pp. 295 and 296). — One shall not be able to reproduce the proofs adduced for each of the propositions here enumerated by Maimonides, and one must confine oneself to indicating the passages whence our author has drawn these different propositions. As shall be seen, they are not all borrowed from Aristotle, and several are taken from the works of Ibn-Sînâ, who, as one has already stated elsewhere, is the principal source from which Maimonides drew his knowledge of Peripatetic doctrines. fn.1270: This second proposition enunciates concerning discrete magnitude that which, in the first proposition, was enunciated concerning continuous magnitude. Actual numerical infinity is as inadmissible as infinite extension: for the units which compose discrete quantity may all together form a continuous quantity, and it is clear that, since the latter cannot be infinite, the former can no more be so. One may, moreover, as the commentator Schem-Tob observes, apply directly to this proposition the demonstration which one has given of the first proposition, according to Ibn-Sina. Indeed, by diminishing the discrete quantity, supposed infinite, by a certain number of units, the remainder will be either infinite or finite; now, were it infinite, the part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible; were it finite, the whole would likewise be finite, which is contrary to the hypothesis.

The demonstration given by Aristotle may be summarised thus: Everything that undergoes a change passes from one state of affairs to another; it cannot be for a single instant in either of the two states, for then it would not change; nor can it be wholly in one of the two states, for then it would either not yet be changing, or it would already be changed. fn.1281.sub_0: This proposition, enunciated in too concise a manner, has been deemed obscure, and, taken in an absolute sense, it has encountered objections (vide the commentary of Moses of Narbonne). The following is how it ought to be understood: Everything which has not [[t:0]]within itself[[t:1]] the principle of its motion, but upon which an accidental motion is impressed by an external cause that may cease to exist, will necessarily be at rest when that cause ceass, as, for instance, the passenger of a ship, who is moved only because he is accidentally within a thing in motion, which may cease to move (Cf. Aristotle, [[t:2]]De Anima,[[t:3]] book I, chap. 3, § 2). That which proves Maimonides to apprehend this proposition thus, is that further on, at the commencement of chapter I, in demonstrating that the prime mover cannot be considered as the soul of the celestial sphere, he applies this VIII[[t:4]]th[[t:5]] proposition to the human soul, which is moved [[t:6]]accidentally[[t:7]] with the body by an external cause, whether in seeking that which is agreeable unto it, or in fleeing that which is contrary unto it. It is therefore erroneously that the Arabic commentator Al-Tebrîzi objects to this proposition of Maimonides, averring that there are certain motions which, albeit accidental, are nonetheless perpetual, as, for example, the diurnal motion from East to West, impressed by the ninth sphere upon the eight inferior spheres, and which is contrary to their proper and [[t:8]]essential[[t:9]] motion from West to East; or as the circular motion of the sphere of fire and of the other elements, the [[t:10]]essential[[t:11]] motion of which is in a straight line (cf. vol. I of this work, pp. 357-359). It is evident that these accidental motions, having for their cause an essential and perpetual motion, must themselves be perpetual. The proposition here in question appears to relate to a passage in the treatise [[t:12]]On the Heavens[[t:13]] (book I, end of chap. 2), in which Aristotle establishes that above the four elements which, by their nature, possess a rectilinear motion, there exists a simple substance of another nature which possesses circular motion.
fn.1281.sub_1: Now, he observs, this motion must be inherent in the nature of this substance; for it would be astonishing and altogether unreasonable that this motion, which alone is continuous and eternal, could be [[t:14]]contrary to nature[[t:15]], inasmuch as, in general, that which is contrary to nature is swiftly destroyed: E[[t:16]]ἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν φέρεται τά φερόμενα ϰύϰλῳ τὴν περὶξ φοράν, θαυμαστὸν ϰαὶ παντελῶς ἀλογον τὸ μόνην εἶναι συνεχῆ τάυτην τὴν ϰὶνησιν ϰαι ἀίδιον, οὖσαν παρὰ, φύσιν · φαίνεται γὰρ ἔν γε τοῖς ἀλλοις τάχιστα φθειρόμενα τὰ παρὰ φύσιν[[t:17]]. The Arabic version, which rendered the words [[t:18]]contrary to nature[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]παρὰ φύσιν[[t:21]]) by [[t:22]]accidental[[t:23]], does better explicate the terms of Maimonides' proposition. Behold how the passage we have just cited has been paraphrased in the middle commentary of Ibn-Roschd, [[t:24]]De Cœlo et Mundo,[[t:25]] book I, [[t:26]]summa[[t:27]] IV, [[t:28]]demonstrat.[[t:29]] 5 (Hebrew version): [[t:30]]והוא שזאת התנועה הסבובית שהיא סביב האמצע לא המלט משתהיה לזה הגשם טבעית או מקרית ושקר הוא שתהיה מקרית בי התנועה המקרית אי אפשר שתמצא תמידית אין תכלית לה ושהצעת זה יוצאה מכל הקש כי אנחנו רואים הדברים המקריים כלים אובדים[[t:31]].
fn.1282: This proposition has been extensively developed by Aristotle, who, in order to establish the existence of a prime unmoved mover, demonstrats that that which movs, if it be not the prime mover itself, can be but an intermediate cause of motion, which is necessarily moved itself by another cause. It follows naturally that the physical body cannot communicate motion to another body save by being moved itself. Vide [[t:0]]Physica[[t:1]]., book VIII, chap. 5; Cf. [[t:2]]Metaphysica[[t:3]]., book XII, chap. 6.
fn.1285: That is to say: what one does designate [[t:0]]a force in a body[[t:1]] may be either an accident, as for example heat and coldness in bodies which, by their nature, are neither hot nor cold, or indeed a physical form, such as, for instance, the heat or the igneous nature of fire, or the coldness of ice. The word [[t:2]]قوة[[t:3]] (potency), which the Arabian philosophers employ in the various senses that Aristotle attributs to the word [[t:4]]δύναμɩς[[t:5]], must be taken here not in the sense of [[t:6]]possibility[[t:7]] or [[t:8]]faculty of being[[t:9]] as opposed to [[t:10]]act[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]ἐνέργεɩα[[t:13]]), but in its primitive and absolute sense which Aristotle defins as «the principle from which emanats motion or change produced in another thing inasmuch as it is another thing» ([[t:14]]Metaphysica[[t:15]]., book V, chap. 12, commencement and end), or in other words, in the sense of [[t:16]]force[[t:17]] or of [[t:18]]active faculty[[t:19]]. This force may be found outside the body upon which it acts, or within that body itself; and in this latter case, it is a [[t:20]]force in a body[[t:21]].
fn.1287: The more precise meaning of this proposition is as follows: amongst the accidents or qualities which subsist only within the body, there are some which divide with the body, such as, for instance, the heat of a warm body or the colour inherent in a body; for every particle of the body retains the same heat and the same colour. Others do not follow the division of the body, such as, for instance, figure, which does not always remain the same when the body is divided. On the other hand, even amongst those things which constitute or perfect the being of the body, there are some which cannot be divided in any manner, neither in reality nor even in thought, and such pre-eminently are the rational soul and the intelligence; others, like certain physical forms, divide with the body to which they belong. — By [[t:0]]soul[[t:1]] and [[t:2]]intelligence[[t:3]], the author signifies not only the rational soul of man and the [[t:4]]hylitic intellect[[t:5]], but also the souls of the celestial spheres and the intelligence by which they [[t:6]]conceive[[t:7]] the particular aim of their motion: for it will be seen further on (chap. IV) that the author, following the theory of Ibn-Sīnā, attributes to the celestial spheres not only a soul, but also a thought inherent in them, which must not be confounded with the [[t:8]]separated intelligences[[t:9]] which are the object of desire for their respective spheres, and which determine their motion.
fn.1288: Aristotle, having established that the prime mover is not moved, endeavours to demonstrate that it possesses neither parts nor extension. Starting from the proposition already demonstrated, that there is no infinite extension or magnitude, he shows that the prime mover cannot be a finite magnitude, for the motion emanating from it being infinite, it would follow that [[t:0]]in a finite magnitude there can be an infinite force;[[t:1]] yet, this is impossible, for infinite force ought to produce its effect in a time less than that which any finite force would require to produce the same effect, that is to say, infinite force would produce its effect in no time or instantaneously, which is inadmissible, as every transformation occurs within a certain time. Will it be said that infinite force also produces its effect within a certain time? But then one could discover a finite force which would produce the same effect in the same time, and it would follow that this finite force would be equal to an infinite force, which is impossible. Such is, in substance, the demonstration by which Aristotle establishes that [[t:2]]in a finite magnitude there cannot be an infinite force[[t:3]]. See [[t:4]]Physics[[t:5]], book VIII, ch. 10 (Bekker's ed., p. 266 [[t:6]]a[[t:7]]): [[t:8]]ὅτι δ’ὅλως οὐϰ ἐνδέχεται ἐν πεπε-ρασμένῳ μεγέθει ἄπειρον εἶναι δύναμιν, ἐϰ τῶνδε δῆλον. ϰ. τ. λ.[[t:9]]
fn.1290: The first three kinds of changes enumerated above (prop. IV) all indicate the passage from one state to another opposite state; now, the two opposite states are necessarily separated one from the other by an interval of time, and consequently the change is not continuous. Nothing of the like takes place in the fourth kind of change, or in local motion, which alone can be continuous. See Arist., [[t:0]]Phys[[t:1]]., book VIII, ch. 7 (p. 261 [[t:2]]a[[t:3]]): ὅ[[t:4]]τι μὲν οὖν τῶν ἄλλων ϰινή-σεων οὐδεμίαν ἐνδέχεται συνεχῆ εἷναι, ἐϰ τῶνδε φανερόν[[t:5]]. Ἅ[[t:6]]πασαι γὰρ ἐξ ἀντι-ϰειμένων εὶς ἀντιϰείμενά εἰσιν αἱ ϰινήσεις ϰαὶ μεταϐολαὶ, ϰ. τ. λ.[[t:7]] Cf. [[t:8]]ibid.,[[t:9]] book V, chap. 4 (p. 228 [[t:10]]a[[t:11]], [[t:12]]b[[t:13]].): Κ[[t:14]]εῖται γὰρ τὸ συνεχές, ὧν τὰ ἔσχατα ἕν... πολλαὶ οὖν ϰαὶ οὐ μία ἡ ϰίνησις, ὧν ἐστίν ὴρεμία μεταξύ[[t:15]].
fn.1291: In local motion itself, only circular motion is truly continuous; for motion in a straight line, being unable to continue to infinity, must necessarily have a stopping point from which it will turn, either to take another direction, or to return in the opposite direction. See [[t:0]]ibid[[t:1]]., book VIII, chap. 8, at the beginning: [[t:2]]Ὅτι δ’ἐνδἑχεται εἶναί τινα ἄπειρον, μίαν οὖσαν ϰαὶ συνεχῆ, ϰαὶ αὔτη ἐστίν ἡ ϰύϰλῳ, λέγωμεν νῦν... ὅτι δὲ τὸ φερόμενον τήν εὐθεῖαν ϰαὶ πεπερασμένην οὐ φέρεται συνεχῶς, δῆλον. ’Α’ναϰάμπτει γάρ, τὸ δ’ ἀναϰάμπτον τὴν εὐθεῖαν τὰς ἐναντίας ϰινεῖται ϰινήσεις[[t:3]]. See also [[t:4]]Metaphysics[[t:5]]., book XII, chap. 6, where our proposition is enunciated in these terms: [[t:6]]Κίνησις δ’οὐϰ ἔστι συνεχής ἄλλ’ ἢ ἡ ϰατὰ τόπον, ϰαὶ ταύτης ἡ ϰύϰλῳ[[t:7]].
fn.1293.sub_0: In this proposition, the author establishes that local motion (that, of course, which, in the preceding proposition, was designated as the sole continuous one) is prior [[t:0]]in nature[[t:1]] to all other motions and changes; and by [[t:2]]prior in nature[[t:3]] one must understand, conformably to Aristotle's definition ([[t:4]]Metaph[[t:5]]., book V, chap. 11), that which can exist without other things existing, but without which other things cannot exist. The terms of this proposition are drawn from Aristotle's [[t:6]]Physics[[t:7]], book VIII, chap. 7 (Cf. book VII, chap. 2), although the author, it would appear to one, does not strictly follow the Stagirite's reasoning. It has been observed above, p. 6, note 2, that according to Aristotle, the idea of motion applies to the categories of quantity, quality, and place. Now, he says, of these three species of motion, that of place is necessarily the first: for it is impossible that there should be [[t:8]]growth[[t:9]] without there having first been [[t:10]]transformation.[[t:11]] Transformation is the change into that which is opposite; but when there is transformation, it is necessary that there be something which transforms and which causes, for example, that which is potentially hot to become actually hot. Now it is evident that the mobile of this transformation is sometimes nearer and sometimes further from the thing to be transformed, and that transformation could not occur without local motion; this, consequently, is the first among motions. Further on, Aristotle establishes by other proofs that local motion, although it be the last to develop in the individual beings of this world, is the first in the universe and even precedes the generation ([[t:12]]γένεσις[[t:13]]) of all things, which is followed by transformation and growth ([[t:14]]μετὰ γὰρ τὸ γενέσθαι πρῶτον ἀλλοίωσις ϰαὶ αὔξησɩς[[t:15]]; [[t:16]]Phys[[t:17]]., VIII, 7, pag. 260 [[t:18]]b[[t:19]], line 32).
fn.1293.sub_1: One might at first be surprised that Maimonides places transformation before generation and corruption; but it appears that our author considers transformation from a more general standpoint, that is to say, not only in relation to the category of quality, as in the IV[[t:20]]th[[t:21]] proposition, but also in relation to [[t:22]]generation[[t:23]], which is itself in some sort a transformation of matter by form, a transformation wrought by an agent more or less remote, which needs to approach the matter to be transformed. It is also in this sense that Ibn-Roschd explains the passage from the [[t:24]]Physics[[t:25]]. See Aristotle's Works with Averroës' Commentaries, folio edition, t. IV, fol. 180 [[t:26]]c[[t:27]]: «[Lat.: Then he says: [[t:28]]And it is manifest that the disposition of the mover then does not run in the same way[[t:29]], [[t:30]]but perhaps sometimes it will be nearer to the altered and sometimes further away[[t:31]], etc. That is, and because the first altering thing, which is not altered, does not always alter, but sometimes, it is necessary that it not hold itself with the altered in the same disposition, but sometimes it approaches it, and alters, and sometimes it withdraws, and does not alter: and proximity, and distance is not, except by translation: therefore translation naturally precedes alteration, namely that, when both have been in act: then the altering thing altered, after it was not altering: it is necessary that one move in place either the altering, or the altered, or both. If, however, one has been [[t:32]]generated[[t:33]], or both, and we have posited this to be the cause of that, which sometimes alters, and sometimes does not, [[t:34]]it will be manifest that translation ought to precede in the same way, since alteration also precedes generation; for generation is either alteration or follows alteration[[t:35]].]»

fn.1299: See Arist., [[t:0]]Phys[[t:1]]., book VII, chap. 1: Ἅ[[t:2]]παν τὸ ϰινούμενον ἀνάγϰη ὑπό τινος ϰινεῖσθαɩ[[t:3]]. Aristotle demonstrates this proposition by arguing chiefly from the infinite divisibility of that which is moved (See the VIII[[t:4]]th[[t:5]] propos.), which does not permit one to stop at any part whatsoever of the moved thing to perceive therein the motor principle of the whole; whence it follows that this mover is necessarily something other than the entirety of the moved thing. Cf. book VIII, chap. 6, towards the end.
fn.1305: This proposition results from the combination of propositions V and XVII. Movement having been defined as the passage from potency to act (cf. [[t:0]]Phys[[t:1]]., III, 1 and 2; [[t:2]]Metaph[[t:3]]., XI, 9), and every movement presupposing a mover which is other than the thing moved, it thence follows that everything in potency requires an external impulse to pass into act. Potency is a faculty of acting or a faculty of receiving action (cf. [[t:4]]Metaph[[t:5]]., IX, 1); in both cases, potency passes into act only by virtue of something which proceeds from without. Thus, for instance, the artist, who possesses the faculty of producing a work of art, requires an external material to realise this faculty; and similarly, bronze, which possesses the faculty of becoming a statue, requires the artist's labour for this faculty to be realised.
fn.1308: Literally: [[t:0]]and understand this[[t:1]]. Commentators observe that the author here adds these words on account of the profound import of this proposition, which appears to subvert the dogma of creation: for God, being absolute energy always in act, and nothing being capable of obstructing His action, could not, at a given moment, have created the world, or passed from potency to act. See, upon this question, chapter XVIII of this II[[t:2]]e[[t:3]] part.
fn.1309: This proposition and the two succeeding ones are borrowed from Ibn-Sinâ, who was the first to make, within the idea of [[t:0]]necessary being[[t:1]] (as opposed to the absolute [[t:2]]possible[[t:3]], which comes into being and perishes), this distinction between that which is [[t:4]]necessary in itself[[t:5]] or the absolute necessary, and that which is [[t:6]]necessary through another[[t:7]], being by its own essence in the category of the possible. Of the second species are, according to Ibn-Sinâ, the celestial spheres, in which one distinguishes potency and act, matter and form, and which derive the quality of [[t:8]]necessary beings[[t:9]] solely from their relation to the first cause, or God. Ibn-Sinâ departs, in this respect, from Aristotle, who expressly extends the idea of [[t:10]]necessary being[[t:11]] to that which is moved eternally, or to the celestial spheres, which, he states, are in no wise in potency and possess no matter properly so-called, that is to say, no matter subject to generation and corruption. See [[t:12]]Metaph[[t:13]]., book IX, chapter 8: O[[t:14]]ὐθέν ἂρα τῶν ἀφθάρτων ἁπλῶς δυνάμει ἐστὶν ὄν ἁπλῶς οὐδὲ τῶν ἐξ ἀνὰγϰης ὄντων, ϰαί τοι ταῦτα πρῶτα.... διὸ ἀεὶ ἐνεργεῖ ἥλιος ϰαὶ ἄστρα ϰαὶ ὅλος ὁ οὐρανὸς, ϰ. τ. λ[[t:15]]. fn.1311: That is to say, the relation between cause and effect, or the necessary condition under which alone a given cause produces a given effect. «Everything,» states Ibn-Sinâ ([Lat.: loco citato]), «whose existence is necessary through another, is in itself of a possible existence: for the necessity of its existence depends upon a certain [[t:0]]relation[[t:1]] [[t:2]](نسبة)[[t:3]] , in which one considers something other than the very essence of the thing in question.» Thus, for instance, the sun becomes the cause of day for a part of the earth only when it is found in a certain position relative to that part.
fn.1313: It is evident, and the author frequently insists thereupon (See, in volume I, the chapters concerning the attributes, and hereinafter, ch. I), that the absolute and necessary being cannot be composed of two distinct things, and that thought cannot even therein distinguish two distinct ideas, or two intelligible things. Consequently, every existence which presents itself, in our thought, as a compound of two ideas, as for example matter and form, cannot be, as it presents itself, [[t:0]]necessary in itself[[t:1]], inasmuch as it is, at the very least for thought, the result of a composition: for, as Ibn-Sinâ observes, it is impossible to admit that the whole is, by its essence, anterior to the parts, but it is either posterior, or coexistent therewith.
