fn.1314: The notions of potency and act, of matter and form, are so familiar to the Peripatetics that the proposition here in question requires no explanation. It is merely to be observed that the author here understands by [[t:0]]body[[t:1]], not only that which is subject to generation and corruption, but also the celestial bodies; these, according to Aristotle, whilst not possessing matter susceptible of generation, do possess one which serves as a substratum for translatory motion. See Arist., [[t:2]]Metaph.[[t:3]], IX, 8, at the end, and XII, 2, and Cf. [[t:4]]Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe[[t:5]], p. 4, note 1, and p. 18, note 1. Maimonides adopted the opinion of Ibn-Sina, who purported to furnish a general demonstration of the existence of matter and form in bodies, applicable to [[t:6]]all bodies[[t:7]], including the celestial spheres. Cf. Schahrestàni, p. 366 (Germ. trans., II, p. 239-240). This opinion, by which one might be led to attribute to the celestial bodies also an [[t:8]]being in potency[[t:9]] (which would be contrary to Aristotle's theories), was contested by Ibn-Roschd; the latter considers the celestial bodies as simple bodies which discover their form or their entelechy in the [[t:10]]separated intelligences[[t:11]]. Cf. Ibn-Falaquéra, [[t:12]]Moré ha-Moré[[t:13]], on this proposition (p. 71-72).
fn.1316:
There is a nuance between [[t:0]]potency[[t:1]] and [[t:2]]possibility;[[t:3]] the former may exist solely in our thought, whilst the latter inheres in the things themselves. Thus, one often distinguishes potency and act in a purely ideal manner, even when in reality the two notions are inseparable one from another; prime matter, for instance, is a [[t:4]]potency[[t:5]], but this potency exists separately only in thought, for prime matter is inseparable from form. [[t:6]]Possibility[[t:7]], on the contrary, resides in the object itself, and designates that which may or may not be; thus, for example, bronze may or may not be a statue, and the statue may cease to be what it is by losing its form. Thus, then, the author who seeks to characterize, in this proposition, that which, at a certain moment, may not exist in act, must add to [[t:8]]potency[[t:9]] the condition of [[t:10]]possibility[[t:11]] within the very essence of the thing, intending thereby that whatsoever is in potency, not merely in our thought, but because the thing itself encompasses the notion of the [[t:12]]possible[[t:13]], may also be conceived as not existing in act at a certain moment. In sum, this proposition reverts to what Aristotle declared, namely, that whatsoever is [[t:14]]possible[[t:15]] may not be in act, and consequently it may both be and not be. See [[t:16]]Metaphysics[[t:17]], Book IX, Chapter 8 (Brandis's edition, p. 187-188): Ἕ[[t:18]]στι δ’οὐθὲν δυνάμει ἀΐδιον..... Tὸ δυνατὸν δὲ πᾶν ἐνδέχεται

fn.1374.sub_0: This demonstration appears to be founded upon a passage in Aristotle's [[t:0]]Physics[[t:1]], which may be summarised thus: In motion, three things may be considered: that which is moved, that which moves, and that by which the latter moves. That which is moved does not necessarily impart motion; that which serves as an instrument or intermediary imparts motion whilst simultaneously receiving it; lastly, that which moves without being an instrument or intermediary is itself immobile. Now, as one observes (in the universe), on the one hand, that which is moved without possessing within itself the principle of motion, that is to say, without moving aught else, and on the other hand, that which is at once moved by another and is itself the mover of another, it is reasonable, if not necessary, to admit of a third entity which moves without being moved. See [[t:2]]Phys.[[t:3]], Book VIII, Ch. 5 (Bekker's edit., p. 256 [[t:4]]b[[t:5]]): [[t:6]]τρία γὰρ ἀνάγϰη εἶναι, τό τε ϰινούμενον, ϰαὶ τὸ ϰινοῦν, ϰαὶ τὸ ᾧ ϰινεῖ. ϰ. τ. λ.[[t:7]] In the [[t:8]]Metaphysics[[t:9]], Book XII, Chapter VII, Aristotle himself summarises thus: [[t:10]]ἔστι τοίνυν τι ϰαὶ ὅ ϰινεῖ, ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ ϰινούμενον ϰαὶ ϰινούν, ϰαὶ μέσοντοίνυν ἐστί τι ὃ οὐ ϰινούμενον ϰινεῖ, ἀΐδιον ϰαὶ οὐσία ϰαὶ ἐνέργεια οὖσα[[t:11]]. Alexander of Aphrodisias explained this passage in terms nigh identical to those employed by Maimonides in this second demonstration; and it is doubtless from Alexander that our author borrowed his argumentation, as well as the proposition which he places at the head as having been enunciated by Aristotle himself. Alexander’s explanation was cited by Averroes in his grand commentary upon the [[t:12]]Metaphysics[[t:13]]. One reproduces it from the Latin version of this commentary (edit. in-folio, f. 149 [[t:14]]verso[[t:15]]): «[Lat.: Dixit Alexander: Ista est ratio quod [est] aliquod movens [quod] non movetur, et est dicta breviter et rememoratio ejus quod dictum est in ultimo Physicorum. Et est fundata super duas propositiones, quarum una est quod omne compositum ex duobus quorum alterum potest esse per se, possibile erit etiam alterum esse per se, nisi compositio sit substantiæ et accidentis; verbi gratiâ quod hydromel, quia componitur ex aqua et melle, et mel invenitur per se, necesse est ergo ut aqua inveniatur per se. Et, quia invenimus aliquod motum et movens quasi compositum ex movente et moto, et invenimus aliquod motum per se et non movens, manifestum est quod est necesse aliquod movens esse et non motum.]
fn.1374.sub_1: [Lat.: Hoc igitur movens immune est a potentia, et in nulla materia existit.]» As for the proposition attributed by Maimonides to Aristotle, some commentators have objected that, in that which is composed of [[t:16]]substance[[t:17]] and [[t:18]]accident[[t:19]], one cannot conceive of the existence of the accident alone, albeit the substance may evidently exist alone. This objection falls away by virtue of the express condition posited by Alexander: [Lat.: nisi compositio sit substantiœ et accidentis[[t:21]]]. Maimonides, in copying Alexander, may perchance have omitted this condition through inadvertence.

fn.1377: The author, interrogated by the translator Ibn-Tibbon concerning the precise meaning of this passage, explains himself almost thus in the letter cited above: When the [[t:0]]possible[[t:1]] is predicated of a species, it is requisite that it should exist actually in certain individuals of that species; for, were it never to exist in any individual, it would be [[t:2]]impossible[[t:3]] for the species, and by what right, then, could it be said to be [[t:4]]possible?[[t:5]] If, for example, one avers that writing is a thing possible for the human species, it is necessarily consequent that there should be men who write at some given time; for, should it be contended that there is never any man who writes, this would be tantamount to affirming that writing is impossible for the human species. It is not so with the [[t:6]]possible[[t:7]] which is predicated of an individual; for, if one says that this child may either write or not write, it does not follow from this possibility that the child must necessarily write at some particular moment. Thus, therefore, the [[t:8]]possible[[t:9]] predicated of a species is not, strictly speaking, within the category of the possible, but is in some wise [[t:10]]necessary[[t:11]]. — This explanation does not yet suffice to convey a clear apprehension of the conclusion which the author is about to draw from this proposition, to wit, that all beings would have necessarily perished. There is here, perchance, an obscure point upon which the author was unwilling to express himself more clearly, as indicated by the commentator Ephodi. Cf. the introduction to the first part, vol. I, p. 28, VII[[t:12]]th[[t:13]] cause. According to the indications of the commentator Schem-Tob, the author’s thought would be thus: the possibility attributed to an entire species is, like the species itself, an eternal thing; one cannot, strictly speaking, attribute a possibility to an eternal thing, and for such a thing, all that is possible shall be at the same time necessary. — In a word, the author evidently intended to convey that the hypothesis of contingency, for the universality of beings, is inadmissible; and if he did not clearly state this thesis, it is perchance because he feared to offend certain readers, by explicitly acknowledging that this demonstration, which he declares to be the strongest, is founded upon the principle of the eternity of the world.

fn.1394: This method aims to demonstrate that, every body being composite, God, who is absolute simplicity, cannot be a body. It is comprised of two distinct demonstrations. fn.1527.sub_0: The four astronomical terms here employed by the author are borrowed from the theories of Ptolemy concerning the motion of the planets. By [[t:0]]اختلاف[[t:1]] is designated [[t:2]]anomaly,[[t:3]] or the inequality of a celestial body; the word [[t:4]]رجوع[[t:5]] designates the apparent [[t:6]]retrogradation[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]προήγησις[[t:9]]) of the five planets, opposed to their [[t:10]]direct motion[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]ὑπόλειψις[[t:13]]) designated in Arabic by the word [[t:14]]استقامة[[t:15]], [[t:16]]rectitude;[[t:17]] finally, by [[t:18]]إقامة[[t:19]], one understands what Ptolemy terms the [[t:20]]station[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]στηριγμός[[t:23]]) of these same planets, that is to say, the position in which the motion of the celestial body appears to cease. Cf. [[t:24]]Almagest[[t:25]], Book XII, chap. I. In the Arabic version of the [[t:26]]Almagest[[t:27]] (Hebrew MS. of the Imperial Library, ancient collection, no. 441), the terms [[t:28]]προήγησις[[t:29]] and [[t:30]]ὑπόλειψις[[t:31]] are rendered more accurately, the former by [[t:32]]تقدّم[[t:33]] [[t:34]]to go forward,[[t:35]] the latter by [[t:36]]تأخر[[t:37]] [[t:38]]to remain behind.[[t:39]] Later, the Arabs substituted for the former of these two terms that of [[t:40]]رجوع[[t:41]] [[t:42]]retrogradation,[[t:43]] and for the latter that of [[t:44]]استقامة[[t:45]] [[t:46]]rectitude.[[t:47]] Indeed, the periodic motion of the planets occurring from west to east, the planet, when it appears to [[t:48]]retrograde,[[t:49]] i.e., when it appears less advanced in longitude, is found to be forward with respect to the diurnal motion from east to west; the more advanced it is in longitude with respect to the periodic motion, the more it is behind with respect to the diurnal motion. Delambre, to account for the two terms employed by Ptolemy, expresses himself thus ([[t:50]]Notes on the Almagest[[t:51]], appended to the edition of Abbé Halma, Vol. II, p. 16): “One says of a star which preceds another at the meridian, which passes there before it, which marches at its head, that it is [[t:52]]προηγοὐμενος[[t:53]]; of a star which passes there after it, that it is [[t:54]]ἑπόμενος[[t:55]].
fn.1527.sub_1: But that which passes first at the meridian is less advanced in longitude; that which follows it, [[t:56]]ἑπόμενος[[t:57]], which remains behind, [[t:58]]ὑπολειπόμενος[[t:59]], is on the contrary more advanced in longitude; thus a star is [[t:60]]προηγοὐμενος[[t:61]] when its longitude diminishes and it retrograds; [[t:62]]προήγησις,[[t:63]] in the language of the Greeks, therefore corresponds to [[t:64]]retrogradation;[[t:65]] it is the same motion considered with respect to two different points, as, in the theory of curves, one may at will place negative abscissae to the right or to the left of the centre indifferently.” — The terms [[t:66]]retrogradation[[t:67]] and [[t:68]]rectitude[[t:69]] introduced by the Arabs, one also finds them in the [[t:70]]Abridgement of the Almagest[[t:71]] by Ibn-Afla’h, Book VIII, in which the Hebrew version, which alone one is able to consult, has for the former the word [[t:72]]חזרה[[t:73]], and for the latter the word [[t:74]]יושר[[t:75]]. fn.1598.sub_0: One perceives that, according to Maimonides, the difference between Plato and Aristotle is this: that the latter admits not merely the eternity of prime matter, but also that of motion and of time, whereas Plato, whilst admitting the eternity of matter and of chaos, yet believes that the world, as it now exists, had a beginning, that the heavens were, like sublunary things, produced from chaos, and that consequently both motion and time had a commencement. It is in this sense that Plato's opinion has generally been interpreted by the Arabs and by the Scholastics, and it is yet in this sense that one of the most learned adherents of the new Platonic school of Italy does express himself. Herein does Leo Hebraeus express himself on this question ([[t:0]]Dialoghi di amore[[t:1]], III, edit. of Venice, 1572, fol. 145 [Lat.: et seq.]): «Concedendo tutti gli huomini che’l sommo Dio genitore et opifice del mondo sia eterno, senza alcun principio temporale, son divisi nella produttion del mondo, se è ab eterno, o da qualche tempo in quà.
fn.1598.sub_1: Molti dei filosofi tengono essere prodotto ab eterno da Dio, e non havere mai havuto principio temporale, così come esso Dio non l’ha mai havuto, et di questa opinione è il grande Aristolile, et tutti i peripatetici… Ma gli fideli, et tutti quelli che credono la sacra legge di Moise, tengono che’l mondo fusse non ab eterno produtto, anzi di nulla creato in principio temporale, et ancora alcuni dei filosofi par che sentino questo; per quali è il divino Platone, che nel Timeo pone il mondo essere fatto et genito da Dio, produtto del chaos, che è la materia confusa, del quale le cose sono generate… È ben vero che lui fa il chaos, di che le cose sono fatte, eterno, cioè eternalmente produtto da Dio, laquai cosa non tengono gli fideli; perche loro tengono che fino all’ hora della creatione solo Dio fusse in essere senza mondo, et senza chaos, et che l’omnipotentia di Dio di nulla tutte le cose in principio di tempo habbia produtto, che in effetto non par già chiaramente in Moise, che’l ponga materia coeterna a Dio.— Sono adunque tre opinioni nella produttione del mondo da Dio: la prima d’Aristotile, che tutto il mondo fu produtto ab eterno; la seconda di Platone, che solamente la materia, o chaos, fu produtto ab eterno, ma il mondo in principio di tempo; et la terza delli fideli, che tutto sia produtto di nulla in principio di tempo.» — But one does recognise by our passage that in Maimonides' time, as in all epochs, opinions were divided concerning the true import of Plato's doctrine; and, indeed, Plato's poetic language and the mythical garb in which he frequently presents his doctrines do but too well justify this divergence of opinions. Whilst several of the most ancient Platonists, and later the Neoplatonists, maintained that Plato had admitted, like Aristotle, the eternity of the world, others, on the contrary (notably certain Christians, as for instance Clement of Alexandria), went so far as to contend that Plato had professed the doctrine of creation [[t:2]][Lat.: ex nihilo][[t:3]], considering God as the author not merely of the order of the world, but of matter itself. The same divergence is yet to be observed amongst the scholars of our own day. One may consult, in this regard, Zeller, [[t:4]]Die Philosophie der Griechen[[t:5]], vol. II, p. 508 [Lat.: et seq.] (2[[t:6]]nd[[t:7]] edit. Tübingen, 1859), and Henri Martin, [[t:8]]Études sur le Timée de Platon[[t:9]], vol. II, p. 179 [Lat.: et seq.].
fn.1598.sub_2: This latter scholar, after a profound examination of the texts, arrives at conclusions which accord with the opinion of Maimonides and Leo Hebraeus, namely, that according to the [[t:10]]Timaeus[[t:11]], 1° God did not create the prime matter of bodies, that is to say, indeterminate substance; 2° He did not even create second matter, that is to say, eternal chaos; 3° He produced the order of the world, but not from all eternity. — The distinction between incorporeal prime matter and corporeal chaos is of no concern to one here, no more than the question of how Plato understood prime matter and in which his doctrine, in this regard, differs from that of Aristotle. Let it suffice to state that Plato admits an eternal principle opposed to the [[t:12]]Idea,[[t:13]] as blind necessity is to reason, non-being to being, the variable and the multiple to the permanent and the absolute [[t:14]]One.[[t:15]] Yet this is not Aristotle’s [[t:16]]ὕλη[[t:17]], that [[t:18]]being in potency[[t:19]] which necessarily calls for form to become [[t:20]]being in actuality;[[t:21]] for, according to Plato, it is with consciousness and freedom, and not by necessity, that the Idea realises itself in the indeterminate substratum, which it causes to pass from confusion to order. The term [[t:22]]ὕλη[[t:23]] is itself unknown to Plato, although Aristotle employs this term when speaking of his master’s doctrine. This confused and indeterminate substance, which the Idea [[t:24]]orders[[t:25]] and in which it manifests itself, is termed by Plato: [[t:26]]that which receives the impression[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]τὸ ἐϰμαγεῖον[[t:29]]), [[t:30]]that in which things are born, the place[[t:31]], [[t:32]]space,[[t:33]] etc.; it is also presented as [[t:34]]the mother[[t:35]] or [[t:36]]the receptacle and nurse of all generation;[[t:37]] and Plato himself states ([[t:38]]Timaeus[[t:39]], page 49 [[t:40]]a[[t:41]]) that it is a species indeed obscure and difficult to comprehend. Cf. Ritter, [[t:42]]Geschichte der Philosophie[[t:43]], vol. II, pages 347 et seq.; Brandis, [[t:44]]Handbuch der Geschichte der griechisch-römischen Philosophie[[t:45]], vol. II, A, pages 297 et seq.; Zeller, [[t:46]]l. c.[[t:47]], pages 457 et seq.; Henri Martin, [[t:48]]l. c[[t:49]]., vol. I, pages 16 et seq.

fn.1670: Literally: [[t:0]]for one does maintain that,[[t:1]] [[t:2]]after the movement has existed according to that nature upon which it was fixed,[[t:3]] [[t:4]]it is unimaginable that it could have been born and have perished by a total birth and by a total corruption,[[t:5]] [[t:6]]as partial movements are born which are born,[[t:7]] [[t:8]]and as partial movements perish.[[t:9]] The author has expressed himself in an embarrassed and somewhat obscure manner. fn.1708: The author here addresses the direct proofs which may be adduced in favour of creation [Lat.: ex nihilo] [[t:0]]ex nihilo;[[t:1]] he contends against the system of Aristotle, according to which everything in the universe would follow an eternal and immutable law, and he demonstrates that, particularly in the movements of the celestial spheres, one cannot fail to recognise the action of a free will operating with intention and not [[t:2]]by necessity[[t:3]]. This commentary, entitled [[t:6]]שמים חדשים[[t:7]], [[t:8]]the New Heavens[[t:9]], had remained unpublished; it was issued, for the first time, by Wolf Heidenheim, Rödelheim, 1828, in-4°.

fn.1722: According to Abravanel, the author would be alluding to the commentators of Aristotle, and notably to Themistius. The latter had observed that the definition Aristotle gives of the [[t:0]]body[[t:1]], namely that it is that which has length, breadth, and depth (treatise [[t:2]]On the Heavens[[t:3]], book I, chap. These are, therefore, dimensions of another nature, forming bodies of another nature, and consequently it is only by homonymy that the names of [[t:4]]dimension[[t:5]] and [[t:6]]body[[t:7]] are applied simultaneously to the heaven and to sublunary things. fn.1726: The ancients, believing the earth immobile and not generally admitting of its rotation around its axis ([[t:0]]Almagest[[t:1]] I, 6), were obliged to seek another explanation for how it came to pass that the sun and all the planets accomplished, in twenty-four hours, around the earth, a movement from east to west, opposite to the diverse proper motions which they accomplish in longer or shorter periods, transporting themselves from west to east, towards those fixed stars which arrive later at the meridian. It was thus believed that the superior sphere, called the diurnal sphere, alone possessed a natural motion from east to west, in which it carried with it the spheres of the seven planets, which did not prevent the latter from accomplishing their own periodic motion from west to east. See [[t:2]]Almagest[[t:3]], book I, chap. 7, and cf. vol. I of this work, p. 357, note 3. As for the diurnal sphere, there are some among the Arabs who identify it with that of the fixed stars, whilst others make of it a ninth sphere devoid of stars. See above, p. 57, note 3.
fn.1729: The author refers to the superior sphere, which, as one has observed, moves from east to west. He evidently alludes to a passage in the treatise [[t:0]]On the Heavens[[t:1]], book II, chap. 5, where Aristotle seeks to indicate the reason why the heaven moves from left to right; just as, he says, in rectilinear motions (of the elements) that which tends upwards is the noblest, so too, in the circular motions of the celestial spheres, is that which tends forwards or towards the right. It would thus appear that Aristotle speaks here rather of the motion of the planets than of that of the superior heaven; for, [[t:2]]forwards[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]εἰς τὸ πρόσθεν[[t:5]]), or [[t:6]]towards the right[[t:7]], signifies [[t:8]]towards the east[[t:9]]. Cf. [[t:10]]ibid.[[t:11]], chap. 2: [[t:12]]δεξιὸν γὰρ ἑϰάστου λέγομεν, ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴτῆς ϰατὰ τόπον ϰινήσεως · τοῦ δ’ οὐρανοῦ αρχὴν τῆς περιφορᾶς, ὅθεν αἱ ἀνατολαὶ τῶν ἄστρων, ὥστε τοῦτ’ ἂν εἴη δεξιόν, οὗ δ’αἱ δύσεις, ἀριστερόν[[t:13]]. [[t:20]]Manifestum est igitur quare cœlum movetur ex oriente ad occidentem, et non e converso[[t:21]]."]
fn.1730: See [[t:0]]ibid.[[t:1]], chap. 10, where Aristotle states that, the spheres of the planets having a motion opposed to that of the superior heaven, that which is nearest to the latter has the slowest motion, whilst that which is furthest from it has the most rapid motion, and likewise the motion of the others is, by reason of their respective distance from the superior heaven, slower or more rapid: …. [[t:2]]εὔλογον ἤδη τὸ μὲν ἐγγυτάτω τῆς ἁπλῆς ϰαὶ πρώτης περιφορᾶς ἐν πλειστῳ χρόνῳ διιέναι τὸν αὑτοῦ ϰύϰλον, τὸ δὲ πορρωτάτω ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ, ϰ. τ. λ[[t:3]]. — Thus, the periodic revolution of Saturn endures thirty years, that of Jupiter twelve years, and so forth until the revolution of the moon, which is accomplished in less than one month.
fn.1732: Isaac Abravanel reports upon this passage, which is somewhat obscure, the interpretation of another author, which does appear to one exceedingly strained (vide [[t:0]]Schamaïm ’hadaschim[[t:1]], fol. 6). This author conceivs that Maimonides, in averring that there are swifter spheres which are above those possessing the slower motion, intends to speak, on the one hand, of the periodic motions peculiar to the respective spheres of each planet, and, on the other, of the motions of the apogees of the planets inferior to it; for the precessional movement of these apogees is well-nigh as slow as that of the sphere of the fixed stars. Now, it is evident that the sphere of Saturn, for instance, is nearer to the eighth sphere than the apogee of Jupiter, and a fortiori than that of Mars and the other planets; in like manner, the sphere of Jupiter is more exalted than the apogee of Mars, and so forth. If, furthermore, Maimonides declare that there are spheres possessing equal motions, albeit they be above one another, the same author deems that he intends to speak of these self-same apogees which all, it appears, possess equal motions, with the exception of those of Mercury and the moon; or else, of the periodic revolutions of the sun, Venus, and Mercury, which were believed to be of equal duration. — Yet, it is not probable that Maimonides should have compared movements of so diverse a nature amongst themselves. It may be that in stating that certain spheres possessing the swifter motion are above those possessing the slower motion, he intends to speak of the planet Mercury, which, according to an opinion appearing probable to him (vide supra, chap. IX), is situated above the sun, and whose true periodic motion is of shorter duration than that of the sun; for unto it was attributed a duration of approximately ten months. (Vide Abravanel, [[t:2]]l. c.[[t:3]]) By the planets with equal motions and whose periodic motion is accomplished in the same space of time or nearly so, Maimonides perhaps understands Venus and the sun. Nevertheless, one dare affirm naught in this regard; for there is much divergence in the data found amongst Arabic astronomers concerning the periodic revolutions of Mercury and Venus, and it would be requisite to ascertain what data were adopted by Maimonides. Cf. [[t:4]]Almageste[[t:5]], book IX, chap. III et seq.

fn.1737: This passage is drawn from the treatise [[t:0]]On the Heavens[[t:1]], book II, chapter 12, in which Aristotle examins the two following questions: 1° Why the respective motions of each planet do not increase in proportion to their distance from the superior sphere, which has but a single motion? for one observs, on the contrary, that the sun and moon possess fewer motions than the planets situated above, albeit these latter be more distant from the centre and nearer to the superior sphere. 2° Why the superior sphere possesses a great number of stars, whereas each of the inferior spheres has but one? — The Arabic version is but a most free paraphrase of the Greek text, of which one contents oneself with citing the commencement: [[t:2]]δυοῖν δ’ἀπορίαιν οὔσαιν, περὶ ὧν εἰϰότως ἄν ὁστισοῦν ἀπορήσειε, πειρατέον λἑγειν τὸ φαινόμενον[[t:3]]. Which does signify: "As there exist two difficulties which might, with good right, perplex anyone, it is needful to endeavour to say [[t:4]]what appears to us[[t:5]]." One perceivs that the words [[t:6]]τὸ φ ανόμενον[[t:7]], [Lat.: id quod videtur][[t:9]], have been paraphrased, in Arabic, by [[t:10]]that which our intelligence comprehends[[t:11]], [[t:12]]our science and our opinion[[t:13]]. Maimonides has, therefore, taken needless pains, in explaining further on, in a most subtle manner, what Aristotle intended by the three words [[t:14]]intelligence[[t:15]], [[t:16]]science[[t:17]] and [[t:18]]opinion;[[t:19]] for not a single one of these words is to be found in the Greek text. — The two Arabo-Latin versions of the treatise [[t:20]]On the Heavens[[t:21]] do not possess the word [[t:22]]intelligence[[t:23]]. That of Michael Scott (published under the name of [[t:24]]Paul Israélite[[t:25]]) bears: "[Lat.: Et volumus modo perscrutari de duabus quæstionibus, de quibus oporlet perscrutatorem perscrutari; et dicemus in eis [[t:26]]secundum nostram scientiam et nostram opinionem[[t:27]].]" The other version, anonymous and inedited (Latin manuscript of the Imperial Library, Saint-Victor collection, n° 872, fol. 147), has the following terms: "[Lat.: Volo autem nunc inquirere de duabus quæstionibus inquisitione sufficiente; convenit autem ut inquirat de his inquisitor. Dicam ergo in utrisque [[t:28]]secundum summam scientiœ nostrœ et nostrœ sententiœ[[t:29]].]"
fn.1739: Vide supra, p. 153, note 1. Concerning the reason why the spheres possess a slower motion in proportion as they approach more closely to the superior (diurnal) sphere, Aristotle expresses himself in these terms ([[t:0]]De Caelo[[t:1]], II, 10): [[t:2]]τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐγγυτάτω μάλιστα ϰρατεῖται, τὸ δὲ πορρωτάτω πάντων ἥϰιστα διὰ τὴν ἀπόστασιν[[t:3]]. The import is: that the spheres most approximate to the diurnal motion, which proceeds from orient to occident, are subject to the greatest influence of this motion, insomuch that their contrary motion from occident to orient is more feeble; and, conversely, those which are most remote from the diurnal motion are less impeded in their opposing motion, which, consequently, is more potent and more swift. — This reasoning, indeed, appears rational ([[t:4]]εὔλογον[[t:5]]), as Aristotle affirms. If Maimonides deems it strange and astonishing, it is doubtless because the tardiness or swiftness of the [[t:6]]periodic[[t:7]] motion of the spheres (from occident to orient) is not proportionate to their respective distance from the superior sphere, or else because, according to him, there is one sphere more swift than another, which nevertheless is situated above the latter. The term [[t:8]]מסתגרבה̈[[t:9]], [[t:10]]strange[[t:11]], is not rendered in the Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon, nor in that of Al-’Harîzi.
fn.1741: According to Abravanel ([[t:0]][Lat.: loco citato][[t:1]], fol. 8 [[t:2]]a[[t:3]]), Maimonides alludes to the retrograde motion of the nodes of the planets, which proceeds from orient to occident. Indeed, it is scarcely possible to explain this passage otherwise; for none of the spheres of the planets possesses a natural motion from orient to occident. As spheres were imagined for each motion, so were they also attributed to the retrograde motion of the nodes. Thus, the Arabs assign to the nodes of the moon a sphere which they denominate [[t:4]]فلك الجوزهر[[t:5]], a term rendered by Jewish authors as [[t:6]]גלגל התנין[[t:7]] (vide [[t:8]]Yesôd ’olâm[[t:9]], book III, chap. VIII). Now, the motion of the nodes of the planets situated above the moon is of an extreme tardiness and almost imperceptible, in comparison with the motion of the moon's nodes, which, according to Maimonides, traverse in one year 18°, 44′, 42″ (vide Abridgement of the Talmud, treatise [[t:10]]Kiddousch ha-hodesch[[t:11]], chap. XVI, § 2). However, according to the principles established by Aristotle, the spheres moving from orient to occident ought to possess a more rapid motion, in proportion as they are more approximate to the diurnal sphere and more subject to its influence. Such appears to be the import of Maimonides' objection, however subtle it may seem. Concerning the nodes and their movements, confer Riccioli, [[t:12]][Lat.: Almagestum novum][[t:13]], vol. I, part I, p. 502.

fn.1764: The meaning of this passage is as follows: Aristotle, whilst considering the existence of the world as a [[t:0]]necessary[[t:1]] thing, does not, on that account, believe the world to be the work of blind fatality, nor to have issued from a cause which acts without consciousness of its own operation, as a body which casts a shadow; but he believs, on the contrary, that God acts with full consciousness and is the efficient cause of the world, even as the intellect is the efficient cause of the intelligible, which, as [[t:2]]intelligible[[t:3]], is necessarily thought and comprehended by the intellect.

fn.1823: The ancient astronomers, in order to account for the apparent inequalities in the movements of the planets, posited them to move, at one time, in eccentrics – that is to say, in spheres whose centre deviates from that of the zodiac or of the Earth; at another time, in epicycles – that is, in small secondary spheres, borne by the great concentric or eccentric spheres, the centre of which is supposed to move upon the surface of the great sphere on the circumference of a great circle, termed the [[t:0]]deferent[[t:1]] (Vide [[t:2]]Almagest[[t:3]], Book VI, Chapter 3). These hypotheses, purely geometrical, most ingenious, and at the same time exceedingly complicated, remained throughout the Middle Ages one of the cornerstones of astronomical science. They were rendered superfluous by the discovery of the elliptical orbits of the planets and by that of the laws of attraction. From the commencement of the twelfth century, the Arabian philosophers were disquieted by the improbability of Ptolemy's hypotheses and their lack of conformity with the physical principles and theories of motion expounded by Aristotle. Attempts were made to substitute other hypotheses; however, one did not succeed in elaborating a system capable of contending with that of Ptolemy (Vide my [[t:6]]Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe[[t:7]], pp. 412, 430, 520 et seq.). These attempts met with no success among astronomers, and Maimonides himself, who here assails Ptolemy's hypotheses from a philosophical standpoint, hesitates not, in his treatise [[t:8]]Kiddousch ha-’hodesch[[t:9]], or [[t:10]]On the Fixation of the New Moons[[t:11]], to admit them in their entirety and to take them as the bases for his astronomical calculations.

fn.1837: This proposition is somewhat obscure. The following, as it appears to one, is its purport: The celestial spheres being all precisely nested one within another, without any void existing between them (vide Vol. I, pp. 356-357), it necessarily follows that, of two spheres possessing different centres, the superior, or the greater, shall form on one side upon the lesser an thick arch, whilst, on the other sides, it shall form around the small inner sphere an envelope whose thickness shall progressively diminish, in proportion to the distance between the two centres. It is manifest then that, whenever the great sphere moves around an axis other than that which passes through the two centres, it shall invariably draw the smaller sphere along by its motion. But, if the movement of the great sphere occurs around the axis which passes through the two centres, it shall not be impeded by the inner sphere, which may ever remain in the same position; so that the great sphere may roll around the surface of the smaller, without drawing it along by its movement. — Ibn-Tibbon has expressed himself inaccurately, by stating: [[t:0]]הקוטר העובר בין שני המרכזים[[t:1]]; instead of [[t:2]]בין[[t:3]], one ought to have said [[t:4]]על[[t:5]].

fn.2473.sub_0: Maimonides, in approaching his half-spoken explanation of Ezekiel's vision, in which he seems to rediscover the principal cosmological doctrines of the Arab Peripatetics, deems it necessary to indicate in the first place what one must understand by the four faces attributed to each of the four [[t:0]]’hayyôth[[t:1]], or figures of animals (Ezekiel, I, 10), in which he discerns the celestial spheres, reduced to four: that of the moon, that of the sun, that of the five other planets, and that of the fixed stars. See the II[[t:2]]nd[[t:3]] part of this work at the close of chap. [[t:4]]IX[[t:5]], and chap. [[t:6]]X[[t:7]], p. 82 et seq. The prophet ascribes to the [[t:8]]’hayyôth[[t:9]] a face of man, a face of lion, a face of ox, and a face of eagle, and thus makes them the representatives of that which is most noble among the diverse species of animals. According to our author, the three faces of unreasoning animals are likewise faces of man; but he tells us not why he does insist thereupon, and he leavs us to conjecture what he intends by the symbol of the four faces. One believs that the author alludes to the four causes of the spheres' motion, indicated according to him by the four wings ([[t:10]]v[[t:11]]. 6), and of which he has spoken in chaps. [[t:12]]IV[[t:13]] and [[t:14]]X[[t:15]] of the II[[t:16]]nd[[t:17]] part; these are: the figure of the sphere, that is to say its sphericity, its soul, its intellect by which it conceivs, and the separated Intelligence, the object of its desire (see vol. II, p. 88). In the sublunar world, man is the sole being in whom these four causes of motion are retraced; man alone possesses a soul endowed with conception and an intellect, which are set in motion by the desire to unite with the separated intelligence, that is to say with the universal [[t:18]]active intellect[[t:19]]; and from this point of view, the motion of man has naught in common with that of unreasoning animals and can only be compared to the circular motion of the spheres. Cf. vol. II, chap. [[t:20]]IV[[t:21]], p. 52. The explanation one has just given is indicated by Samuel ibn-Tibbon in his treatise [[t:22]]Yikkawou ha-maïm[[t:23]], chap. XI, p. 47: [[t:24]]וענין הנפש והשכל רמז אליו בשרמז שכלם יש להם פני אדם וכל הפנים פני אדם[[t:25]].
fn.2473.sub_1: One omits other explanations furnished by Moses of Narbonne and Ephodi, which pertain to that which the author has stated concerning the four forces emanating from the four spheres and acting upon the four elements (Vol. II, Chap. fn.2490: One has already seen that the faces and the wings represent, according to the author, the causes of the movement of the spheres. Among these causes, three are inherent in each sphere, namely: its sphericity, its soul, and its intellect; the fourth is the superior Intelligence, the object of desire of each sphere. This fourth cause is an Intelligence [[t:0]]separate[[t:1]] from the sphere, and the various separate Intelligences are likewise distinct among themselves, in that they are the causes and effects of one another. (Vide Vol. II, Introduction, sixteenth proposition, and [[t:2]]ibid.[[t:3]], p. 31, note 2.) Wherefore the prophet says that the faces and the wings were separate [[t:4]]from above[[t:5]], which signifies that the superior causes of movement are separate from their respective spheres and distinct among themselves. Such appears to be the meaning of the obscure words of Maimonides; but he affords us no indication as to the manner in which he interprets the remainder of verse 11: [[t:6]]לאיש שתים חוברות איש ושתים מכסות את גויתיהנה[[t:7]]. Perhaps one ought, according to Maimonides, to translate these words thus: [[t:8]]two[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]wings[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]were attached to each[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]of the ’hayyôth[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]and two covered their bodies[[t:17]], that is to say, two of the motive causes, namely sphericity and the soul, are inherent in each sphere, whilst the two others, as it were, hover above it; for the separate Intelligence, the object of the sphere's desire, is found outside of it, and the intellect which conceivs this desired object is in an intimate relation with it.

fn.2906: The author shows how one has arrived successively at summarising the entire science of God within the science which He possesses of His own essence. In sum, the author distinguishes three opinions concerning divine science: 1° that which admitts that God embraces by a [[t:0]]single[[t:1]] science both varied things and those which daily arise, so that there is in His science neither multiplicity nor change; but according to this opinion, which is that of believers, the science of God would embrace the infinite and non-being. To avoid this difficulty, it has been maintained 2° that divine science extends directly only to stable things, that is to say, to individuals of the superior world and to the genera and species of the sublunary world. In the Qur'an ([[t:12]]II[[t:13]], 59; V, 73; [[t:14]]XXII[[t:15]], 17), the Sabians [[t:16]](الصابيون)[[t:17]] are mentioned alongside the Jews and Christians, as a religious community possessing revealed books and having a share in the life to come. It is generally agreed that the Sabians of the Qur'an are the Mandæans or Christians of Saint John, who, owing to their frequent ablutions, are termed in Syriac [[t:18]]צביעין[[t:19]] (or [[t:20]]צביין[[t:21]], according to the pronunciation of the Mandæans, who suppress the [[t:22]]ע[[t:23]]), that is to say, the [[t:24]]Baptists.[[t:25]] See [[t:26]]E. D. Michaëlis, p. 749. Arabian authors, from the epoch of the Caliph Al-Mamoun, did also bestow the name of Sabians upon the pagans of Harran and of certain other cities in Mesopotamia, who were entirely distinct from the Sabians of the Qur'an, a circumstance which has occasioned much confusion. Vain efforts have been made to discover the etymology of the name [[t:28]]Sabians[[t:29]] as applied to the pagans. The conjecture which has met with the most favour is that of Pococke ([[t:30]]Specimen hist. ar[[t:31]]. [Lat.: Specimen of Arabian History], p. 139), who derivs this name from the Hebrew word [[t:32]]צבא[[t:33]], [[t:34]]army[[t:35]], and who discerns therein an allusion to the worship of the stars termed [[t:36]]צבא השמים[[t:37]], [[t:38]]army of heaven;[[t:39]] but this etymology is no more plausible than all the others.
fn.3123.sub_1: One does now know that there is in reality but a single species of [[t:40]]Sabians[[t:41]], namely the Mandæans; but that the pagans of Harran, menaced with extermination by the Caliph Al-Mamoun, did usurp, circa the year 830 of the Christian era, upon the counsel of a Muslim doctor, the name of Sabians, and did pretend to be the sect mentioned under this name in the Qur'an and recommended by the prophet to the protection of the Muslims. This fact is reported in the [[t:42]]Kitab Al-Fihrist[[t:43]] by Mohammed ben Is’hak al-Nedîm (see the extract from this book furnished by M. de Hammer in the Journal Asiatique, September–October 1841, p. 254 et seq.). It had already been published by Hottinger, [[t:44]]Historia Orientalis[[t:45]] [Lat.: Oriental History], p. 169, and, following him, by Spencer, [[t:46]]De legibus Hebrœorum ritualibus[[t:47]] [Lat.: On the Ritual Laws of the Hebrews], book II, chap. [[t:48]]I[[t:49]], sect. 2 (p. 241 of the Cambridge edition, 1685, folio). It is above all in the work published on the Sabians by M. Chwolson that the fact in question has been brought to light and supported by numerous proofs. The author shows how the name of Sabians, applied in the Qur'an solely to the Mandæans and employed in this sense by Arabian authors, up to the epoch of Al-Mamoun, did subsequently serve to designate likewise the Harranians, and finally, in the VI[[t:50]]th[[t:51]] century of the Hegira, came to be used in the general sense of Pagans. See [[t:52]]Die Ssabier und der Ssabismus[[t:53]] [Ger.: The Sabians and Sabianism] (2 vols. large octavo, St. Petersburg, 1856), vol. I, chap. [[t:54]]VI[[t:55]], p. 139 et seq., and the entirety of chap. [[t:56]]VIII[[t:57]]. This excellent work contains numerous details concerning the religion of the Harranians, which may elucidate several facts reported by Maimonides in this chapter and in the ensuing ones, in which our author aims largely to explain the ceremonial practices prescribed by Moses, by means of the superstitious customs of the Sabians or pagans which the Mosaic laws sought to efface.

fn.3268: This sentence is somewhat obscure; its sense appears to be as follows: The Law being a divine thing, it might seem that it ought to have provided for the absolute good, both of humanity in general and of each individual in particular. But, if one considers nature, which likewise proceeds from God, one will find that it too comprehends all the general advantages which the Law had in view, and yet that there sometimes result from it damages to individuals. Shem-Ṭob cites the following examples: In the legal order, the condemnation of the guilty is a good for society, and yet it may sometimes happen that innocent persons are condemned in consequence of false testimony. In the natural order, rain, necessary for vegetation, is a benefit to humanity, and yet, when too abundant, it can cause severe calamities. One perceives consequently that, both in the legal and in the natural order, God has provided for the general good of society, without regard to individuals who, by exception, are sometimes the victims of the legal or the natural order. This is an incontestable fact which one is not called upon to explain, and which must be attributed to the impenetrable will of the Divinity. — The grammatical construction of this sentence further increases its obscurity; thus the suffix of [[t:0]]פיהא[[t:1]] evidently refers to the word [[t:2]]אלשריעה̈[[t:3]] which stands at the beginning of the sentence, whilst the suffix in [[t:4]]צׄמנהא[[t:5]] refers to the plural: [[t:6]]אלאמור אלטביעיה̈[[t:7]]; the natural construction would therefore be thus: [[t:8]]אלתי פי צׄמנהא תלך[[t:9]] (i.e. [[t:10]]פי אלשריעה̈[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]אלמנאפע אלעאמה̈ אלמוגׄודה̈ פיהא[[t:13]], and in Hebrew: [[t:14]]אשר יש בכללם התועלות ההם הכוללות הנמצאות בה[[t:15]]. Ibn-Tibbon rendered the word [[t:16]]פיהא[[t:17]] by [[t:18]]בהם[[t:19]], whereas it should have been rendered by [[t:20]]בה[[t:21]], that is to say [[t:22]]בתורה[[t:23]]. [[t:0]]XVIII[[t:1]], p. 137.—The reflections contained in this paragraph are rather religious and edifying than rigorously philosophical, and the author could not seriously have believed that they might serve to resolve, [[t:2]]even according to the opinions of the philosophers[[t:3]], all the difficulties presented by the problem of [[t:4]]individual Providence[[t:5]]. This, being an object of religious faith, is not susceptible of philosophical demonstration. The entire book of Job aims to demonstrate that it were a culpable presumption to endeavour to resolve, by means of the reasonings of the intellect, the difficulties of this problem and to lift the veil which covers for us this profound mystery, before which one has but to bow, acknowledging one's impotence. Thus, the author presents his theory as a mere hypothesis, and one must recall what he has said above (chap. [[t:6]]XVII[[t:7]], p. 129): “In this belief, I rely not upon demonstrative proofs, but rather upon that which has appeared to me to be the evident intention of the book of God and of the writings of our prophets, etc.” The translator Ibn-Tibbon, who perceived in the author’s words a more positive assertion (vide the preceding note), drafted upon this matter a lengthy letter to Maimonides to express unto him his doubts. The commencement thereof has been published in the collection of the [[t:8]]Letters of Maimonides[[t:9]] (Amsterdam edition, in-12, 1712, fol. 12 [[t:10]]a[[t:11]]); therein one reads these words: [[t:12]]רק שאלה אחת היא בלבי כאש בוערת עצורה בעצמותי עוררה לי פרק אחד מן הפרקים האחרונים מן החלק השלישי וכו׳[[t:13]]. Ibn-Falaquera has acquainted one with the content of this letter, and he has responded to the doubts expressed by Ibn-Tibbon. Vide the Appendix of the [[t:14]]Moreh ha-Moreh[[t:15]], chap. [[t:16]]II[[t:17]] (pp. 145 et seq.). Moses of Narbonne likewise speaks thereof in his commentary on chap. [[t:18]]LI[[t:19]]. According to him, the author intended to speak of those who (by speculation or by a species of [[t:20]]ecstasy[[t:21]]) have known how to identify themselves completely with the active intellect and to become similar to the separate intelligences, so that, free from the bonds of matter, they cannot be afflicted by any of the evils which strike material beings. The entire letter in question is found in a manuscript of the Bodleian Library (cod.
